Following Trump’s election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. With the new US administration taking office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental shifts on two fronts — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, risks facing emerging market economies have intensified amid a faster pace of US interest rate increases, a stronger US dollar and the possible adoption of trade protectionist measures by the US. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained favourable, and overall loan growth picked up further in the second half of 2016. The residential property market showed signs of adjustment immediately following the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, but has recently rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate increases and, more broadly, US policy uncertainties, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and their potential impact on local interest rates. Following Trump’s election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only did the election result surprise the market, but the ensuing market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that Trump’s tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending and deregulation would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. With the new US administration taking office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental shifts on two fronts — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, Trump’s anticipated tax cuts may not provide the expected stimulus to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity already close to its potential, fiscal stimulus may provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth while exacerbating upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will consequently accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening significantly, long-term bond yields have already risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, rising trade protectionism would create a “lose-lose” outcome for both the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that undermine overall welfare, impede global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the still-fragile recovery of the European economy. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows arising from faster US interest rate increases and further US dollar appreciation has risen. This could weigh on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of abrupt capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns over a sharp rise in energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, leading to broad-based and significant increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate expectations on the sovereign debt markets of 26 selected economies. The findings indicate that the influence of the US Treasury market on sovereign debt markets has strengthened since the 2013 “taper tantrum”, and that US interest rate increases and tightened financial conditions would have significant effects on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016 alongside a recovery in exports, while market volatility, including regional currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields stemming from concerns over possible policy changes by the new US administration, did not gradually stabilise until early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but faces heightened risks and uncertainties. US interest rate increases, regional currency depreciation and increased financial market volatility could result in tightened financial conditions. Meanwhile, the US may pursue protectionist policies, which could affect regional economies, although the actual impact remains unclear. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private-sector business spending. Although the economy continued to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainties remain over the Mainland’s growth outlook. In particular, given the Government’s determination to curb rising housing prices, the property sector may contribute less to growth this year if the property market continues to cool. Meanwhile, continued economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations may add to uncertainties over the near-term economic outlook. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate increases, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private-sector economic activity, concerns remain in the market over the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given that M1 growth accelerated while M2 growth slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) explores the factors that may have led to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings suggest no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, while M1 grew significantly faster than M2 mainly because monetary easing in recent years reduced the opportunity cost of holding liquid money and increased economic uncertainty may have raised precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong’s economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity boosted investment growth in the fourth quarter. Externally, merchandise export growth picked up alongside improving regional trade flows, while exports of services grew steadily on the back of a recovery in trade-related and transportation services. As imports of goods and services grew faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. With economic growth picking up, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. The Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook continues to face significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong’s external demand. Amid appreciation pressure on the US dollar and expectations of faster US interest rate increases, global financial conditions are expected to become less supportive of the real economy and could lead to tightened domestic financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of Hong Kong’s Financial Conditions Index to help monitor domestic financial conditions. Local inflationary pressures have remained moderate since the second half of 2016, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum edged up in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rentals. With import prices stable and domestic cost pressures moderate, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, although it weakened occasionally following the US interest rate increase in December. The Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered. Alongside US dollar appreciation, the nominal effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar rose further. Given the large Monetary Base, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) remained low, but had risen since October due to year-end funding demand and catch-up with the US interest rate increase. Consequently, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the housing loan business, the average mortgage rate edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by stronger domestic economic activity and increased year-end financing demand from multinational corporations. Growth in domestic loans edged up, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after declining slightly in the first half. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew robustly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio edged down to 77.1% at end-2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar LTD ratio declined markedly to 63.8% on strong growth in US dollar deposits. Amid a strong US dollar, both onshore and offshore renminbi (CNH) exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit (CDs)) consolidated further along with other offshore renminbi markets, while volatility in CNH HIBOR increased markedly. Nevertheless, banks’ renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds from uncertainties over the renminbi exchange rate. With improved global market conditions, the Hong Kong equity market closed significantly higher during the review period. Although the US presidential election produced an unexpected result, the market impact was only short-lived. This was mainly because investor expectations of fiscal stimulus under the Trump administration drove global equity markets higher. Although the local market benefited from this, its optimism was tempered by caution, possibly due to concerns over faster US interest rate increases, challenges facing the Mainland’s economic outlook, uncertainties over renminbi policy and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply towards the end of last year and their spread over US Treasury yields widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar debt market expanded steadily during the review period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s CNH debt market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, although new bond issuance for the year as a whole was lower than in the previous year. Looking ahead, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets would come under pressure if global investors reversed their earlier search-for-yield strategies. As US trade policy remains unclear and the renminbi exchange rate may remain volatile, the outlook for these two debt markets over the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties. The residential property market showed signs of adjustment immediately following the Government’s introduction of the new stamp duty measure, but has recently rebounded. In view of renewed market exuberance, the Government raised the stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the following two months. However, transaction volume has risen recently, partly reflecting developers’ increased launches of primary-market units. Meanwhile, property prices continued to reach new highs, although the pace of increase moderated.

The unexpected election of Trump as US President was followed by heightened uncertainty over US policies. While market attention has focused on the short-term benefits of potentially large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity is already close to its potential, and fiscal stimulus may provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth while further increasing upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks facing emerging market economies are rising amid capital outflow pressures stemming from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while possible US trade protectionist measures will also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, with export volumes also increasing recently. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation and possible US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, with increased downside risks to economic growth. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private-sector business spending. The Mainland economy continued to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty surrounding the near-term economic outlook. Given the Government’s determination to curb the rise in housing prices, the property sector’s contribution to economic growth may also decline this year if the property market continues to cool. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Global financial markets reacted strongly to Trump’s unexpected election as US President. In particular, expectations that policies such as tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending and deregulation under Trump would boost US economic growth and inflation drove major equity markets higher (Chart 2.1). As a result, heightened market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes led to a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Chart 2.1 Stock market indices of selected advanced economies. However, the Trump tax cuts anticipated by the market may not have as positive an impact on US economic growth as expected. Although a shift in economic policy towards reliance on fiscal easing would help relieve the heavy burden on monetary easing, whether now is an appropriate time to implement fiscal easing is debatable, given the current stage of the US economic cycle. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap has gradually narrowed, while the unemployment rate in February was in line with the Fed’s estimate of the natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, indicating that US economic activity is close to its potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, in which the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. Indeed, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital may lead to lower tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any event, with less spare capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth could push up inflation, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited. Meanwhile, other factors, including rising oil and commodity prices and potential trade protectionist measures such as the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may also increase upside risks to US inflation. Despite the increased risk of rising US inflation, the Fed remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and was inclined to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market projections for the future federal funds rate have been revised up to levels close to the median Fed projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Fed’s longer-run projection (Chart 2.2). A faster pace of US interest rate hikes could therefore risk triggering significant market volatility. While financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits of stronger US economic growth driven by potentially expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further increase in US government debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfil its election pledge to adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would create market distortions that undermine overall welfare, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future federal funds rate projections: the Fed and the market. In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and drag on the European economic recovery. Although economic conditions in the Euro area improved gradually, with real gross domestic product growing modestly by 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, economic activity in the Euro area remained only slightly above its pre-global financial crisis level, compared with the stronger recovery of the US economy (Chart 2.3). Since the UK’s decision to leave the European Union last summer, the market has been concerned about the eventual break-up of the Euro area. Although Italy’s economic and political situation appeared to stabilise after the formation of a new government and the implementation of measures to rescue the banking sector, the upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) could become political flashpoints amid Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly because of increased political uncertainty, European sovereign bond yields continued to rise and corporate bond spreads widened, particularly in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and weighing on real business investment in the Euro area. Chart 2.3 Real gross domestic product in major advanced economies. In Japan, upward revisions to real gross domestic product in recent quarters showed that the recovery was stronger than previously expected, with year-on-year annual growth rising to 1.6% in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015. However, partly owing to structural problems in the labour market, sluggish wage growth resulted in weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent sharp depreciation of the yen means that the downward pressure on “new core” goods inflation from the earlier yen appreciation will soon begin to ease. Together with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this suggests an improved near-term inflation outlook, with “new core” inflation (excluding fresh food and energy), which fell to 0.1% in December, expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, amid long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain sluggish and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5% – 0.6%, below the level when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014. The risk therefore remains that inflation will fail to reach the Bank of Japan’s medium-term target of 2%. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth through the trade channel may be smaller because of reduced US imports following the global financial crisis and possible US protectionist policies. At the same time, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation will lead to tightened financial conditions, increasing downside risks to the economy. This could weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns about a sharp rise in energy prices, led to a repricing of inflation risks, resulting in a broad-based and significant increase in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of expectations of US interest rate hikes on the sovereign debt markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with regional GDP growing modestly and inflation rising. Real gross domestic product growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable, as private consumption was steady in many regional economies. Meanwhile, exports generally increased modestly from their lows in 2015. This reflected not only stabilising growth in China, but also improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters such as Malaysia and Indonesia, the recovery in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporters, such as South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, also regained momentum on the back of growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — With commodity prices, particularly oil prices, recovering, producer price inflation generally trended upwards. Although this will raise industrial costs and possibly consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may increase as the risk of prolonged deflation recedes. Faster producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, although the actual impact will depend on the extent to which producer price increases are passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the consumer price index indicate that inflation in many regional economies will rise closer to their central banks’ 2017 inflation targets, although it will remain slightly below them (Chart 2.4). Central banks in East Asia generally left their accommodative monetary policy rates unchanged, except for Indonesia, which cut rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline consumer price index inflation, forecasts and central bank targets in East Asia. Despite improvements in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term financial market volatility. Exchange rate market — Following the US presidential election, most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar as investors expected higher US inflation. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies depreciated by less or even appreciated slightly after the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Depreciation of spot exchange rates against the US dollar and changes in nominal effective exchange rates after the US election. Debt and equity markets — Asset prices fell briefly after the US presidential election but soon stabilised. Spreads between sovereign bonds in East Asian economies and US Treasuries increased. However, after markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined, although they did not return to their pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed from their pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign bonds and US Treasuries. Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the “taper tantrum” in mid-2013. Inflows resumed in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain steady, albeit at a pace below its historical average. Given increased uncertainty over US government policies and the Fed’s possible policy response, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. A sharp rise in the US dollar and yields could attract capital from the region to the US, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, particularly those with already high valuations. The resulting tightening of financial conditions would also create repayment pressures for corporates with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. At the macroeconomic level, broad-based global interest rate hikes would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, weighing not only on aggregate demand in the short term but potentially also on longer-term potential growth. Finally, regional exporters face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies under the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in the region’s major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, garments and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these industries have been accompanied by substantial job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and reviving US manufacturing could pose significant risks to the region’s exporters.

Faster growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activities led Hong Kong’s economic growth to pick up slightly in the second half of 2016. Economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017 amid increasing uncertainties in the external environment. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly faster than the 0.8% growth in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and robust labour market conditions, private consumption growth accelerated and became the main driver of GDP growth. Building and construction activities also became buoyant, supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport. However, weak corporate capital spending narrowed the contribution of aggregate investment spending to GDP growth. Externally, both exports and imports of goods grew faster alongside increased regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).22 Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly because of strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to weigh on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). Indeed, unemployment rates in several major sectors declined during the second half, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector stabilised. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment. Coupled with the increase in the Hong Kong dollar (HKD)’s real effective exchange rate arising from a strong US dollar, this will constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Domestically, while stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately as rising interest rates exert a drag. Building and construction activities should grow steadily as housing supply increases and several planned infrastructure projects commence, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will restrain corporate capital spending. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% for 2017, while private-sector analysts’ forecasts average 2.0%. The economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those arising from the external environment. Policy uncertainties under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, with potential protectionist trade policies posing headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar (HKD) fund flows. In addition, US interest rate normalisation will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Although the quarter-on-quarter momentum of local inflation has increased in recent months, inflation has remained moderate overall since the second half of 2016. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index remained steady at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before edging down to 2.4% in January. The increase in inflation momentum was mainly due to higher prices of tradable goods and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods price inflation rose from negative territory in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by basic food and clothing and footwear prices. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, the housing rental component of the composite consumer price index increased as the decline in private housing rentals narrowed and public housing rentals were raised in September 2016, before moderating slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major component Chart 3.6 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals In the near term, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained owing to weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures. Imported inflation should remain low, as the strength of the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) offsets to some extent the impact of the recovery in global commodity prices (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to remain close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby contain inflation in the services component. Despite the tight labour market, wage increases were modest in recent quarters, with real wages per capita rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before declining by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against the backdrop of cautious business sentiment amid persistent uncertainties in the external environment, increases in labour costs should be restrained. In addition, given the lacklustre performance of retail sales in recent months, growth in retail property rentals is expected to be moderate. Moreover, the impact of the earlier easing in private housing rentals will gradually come through, also helping to alleviate inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline for 2017 as a whole, with the Government forecasting an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for the year, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real wages per capita The inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if US inflation rises more rapidly under the Trump administration, the pace of US interest rate increases may be faster than expected, potentially pushing up local mortgage rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. Meanwhile, appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) may keep import prices weak while reducing Hong Kong’s attractiveness to inbound visitors. On the upside, if the global economy expands faster than expected, Hong Kong’s economic growth may accelerate and demand-driven international commodity prices may rise, posing upside risks to local inflation. In addition, the revised statutory minimum wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which may push inflation higher, although the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed through to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose alongside US dollar interbank rates. Partly due to the improving domestic economic environment, total loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalisation, uncertainty over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to broad declines in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released at the meeting of the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on 13–14 December 2016 fuelled market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened alongside other Asian currencies, but began showing signs of weakening as market expectations of a US rate hike in March increased from mid-February. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund-flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators Alongside the strength of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). As the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners had only a modest impact, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) closely tracked the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that non-residents’ investments in equities and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and buoyant initial public offering activities (Table 4.A). However, residents’ debt investments recorded sizeable outflows, partly driven by Hong Kong banks’ increased holdings of US bonds, which more than offset the investment inflows from non-residents. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated portfolio investment outflows in the final quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, together with expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, put pressure on local financial markets and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data indicated inflow pressures on portfolio investment in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to improved global financial market performance as investors remained optimistic about the US adopting expansionary fiscal policies. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process and elections in EU member states may heighten fund-flow volatility. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although the volume of northbound trading exceeded that of southbound trading in the initial period following the launch of Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable and increased further by 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the combined total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained broadly unchanged at the high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within the total, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding EFBNs increased correspondingly, as an additional HK$49.0 billion of Exchange Fund Bills was issued to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base As the domestic economy became more resilient, growth in the Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits registered faster growth of 6.6% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand amid stronger domestic economic activities and a rebound in initial public offering activities. Analysed by counterpart assets, growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively represented money created through credit expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half of the year, US dollar deposits registered a stronger increase of 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). By contrast, deposits in other foreign currencies contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, growth in total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) increased to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, while full-year growth was 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks’ wholesale cost of funding rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained low, they increased partly due to year-end funding demand and a catch-up with the rise in US dollar interbank rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half of the year to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards alongside the US dollar yield curve, with the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at the end of December. In early 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as funding demand eased, while the yield on the long-term Hong Kong Government Bond also edged down alongside US Treasury yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank rates and the 10-year Government Bond yield Given the banking system’s sizeable deposit base, the increase in retail interest rates was relatively small. Banks’ average cost of funding, as measured by the composite interest rate, remained low, rising by only 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). Amid relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage business, the average lending rate for new mortgages declined to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 alongside HIBORs. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Looking ahead, the pace of increases in domestic interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalisation, the scale of capital outflows and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on domestic interest rates, together with a rise in the Hong Kong dollar REER alongside the US dollar exchange rate, may reduce the support provided by domestic financial conditions to the real economy. Box 4 discusses the construction of a Hong Kong Financial Conditions Index for monitoring domestic financial conditions. Amid stronger domestic economic activities and increased demand for cross-border financing, total loans rose further by 4.2% in the second half of the year, following growth of 2.2% in the first half (Chart 4.10). As economic growth momentum strengthened, growth in domestic loans accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after declining slightly in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end funding demand from multinational corporations. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also registered moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayments of foreign currency loans. For 2016 as a whole, total loans grew moderately by 6.5%, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analysed by economic sector, domestic loans recorded mixed performances in the second half of the year (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial concerns and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, reflecting to some extent strong financing demand driven by the better growth prospects of these sectors. Growth in loans to the building and construction and property development sector also accelerated alongside increased private-sector construction activities. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade finance and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans to selected sectors Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half, compared with 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans (including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes) rose by 7.2% (Chart 4.11), partly reflecting the improved economic environment, while growth in residential mortgage loans accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting buoyant residential transactions between July and October. As a result, the household debt-to-GDP ratio also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt-to-GDP ratio and its components Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly stable. Reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio edged down from 78.2% at the end of June 2016 to 77.1% at year-end (Chart 4.13). Meanwhile, the overall foreign currency LTD ratio declined from 61.4% to 59.9% at year-end, with the US dollar LTD ratio falling markedly to 63.8% amid strong growth in US dollar deposits. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit ratios Given expectations of rising interest rates and the rapidly changing macro-financial environment, credit growth will be subject to uncertainty in the period ahead. The HKMA’s “Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook” indicated that loan demand would remain weak in the near term. With the appreciation of the US dollar, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi (CNH) exchange rate traded at a discount to its onshore counterpart for most of late 2016, closing at a yearly low of 6.98 against the US dollar at the end of 2016. The CNH interbank market again experienced liquidity-tightening pressure in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary funding demand ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight CNH HIBOR once surged to 61.3% on 6 January 2017. The rise in CNH funding costs subsequently led to the unwinding of short CNH positions, driving a rebound in the CNH exchange rate in early January 2017 and turning the spread between CNH and onshore renminbi into a premium. Since mid-January, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilised somewhat, liquidity conditions have gradually improved, and the overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fell to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared with the same period in 2015, due to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as lower loan impairment charges. Banks’ capital positions and asset quality also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose notably following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable and low, supported by a large retail deposit base. Nevertheless, banks should prudently assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, particularly the risk of substantial fund outflows and their subsequent potential impact on domestic interest rates. In addition, given the continued increase in the leverage of non-local corporates, a sharp rise in interest rates could lead to deterioration in banks’ asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be raised to 1.875% from 1 January 2018. Retail banks’ profit improved, with the return on assets rising to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 (red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profit was attributable to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as lower loan impairment charges. For 2016 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose to 1.10% from 1.05% in 2015. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Hong Kong’s wholesale funding costs rose notably following the resumption of US interest rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose markedly by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates Nevertheless, the overall impact of the US interest rate hike on retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained modest. This was because retail deposits were the main source of funding for retail banks, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low despite the interest rate hike. Against this background, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016 after remaining at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar picture. While banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars increased by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the average cost of deposit funding in the retail market rose by a smaller 11 basis points. Overall, licensed banks’ average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs increased by 17 basis points (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The magnitude and speed of the rise in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates exceeded those of Hong Kong banks’ funding costs, which might benefit some retail banks. This was because they had actively promoted housing loans priced with reference to the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate in recent years, and higher interest rates on such loans might help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins might be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there were signs that some banks had reduced the spreads of their mortgage rates over the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. Over the longer term, with further US interest rate hikes, banks might soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and exerting a more significant impact on net interest margins. Banks’ capitalisation remained strong and well above the international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a high level of 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated position. 2. The revised Basel III capital adequacy framework applicable to locally incorporated authorized institutions took effect on 1 January 2013. Therefore, capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. The liquidity position of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the reporting period. Although the average Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) of category 1 institutions edged down to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016, it remained at a high level (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained well above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector was able to withstand liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for retail banks. The share of customer deposits in banks’ total liabilities rose to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks As retail banks’ total loans and advances and total deposits grew at similar rates during the reporting period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). During the same period, the Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratios also remained broadly unchanged. Chart 5.8 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of retail banks Although the interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks increased slightly, it remained at a low level. Estimates indicated that, under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions could decline by an amount equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base in December 2016 (Chart 5.9). However, given that the pace of US interest rate normalisation could be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail banks’ loan portfolios remained sound, with the gross classified loan ratio and overdue and rescheduled loans ratio remaining low at 0.72% and 0.53%, respectively, at the end of December 2016. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks Although current asset quality remained sound by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to monitor the external environment closely. As the assessment in Box 5 shows, the banking sector’s loans for use outside Hong Kong grew rapidly after the global financial crisis, indicating that banks’ asset quality had become more susceptible to the external environment. Banks had mixed expectations about near-term credit growth. According to the HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2016, although most surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the following three months, the share of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the following three months edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk associated with unsecured personal loans remained contained, with the annualised credit card charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24%, respectively, at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio for credit card lending and bankruptcy petitions Banks’ housing loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at the end of December. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of new mortgages was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio was well below the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt servicing index for new mortgages47 rose to 48.8 in the fourth quarter of 2016 from 44.0 in the second quarter (red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average size of new mortgages (Chart 5.13). Continued US interest rate normalisation could further increase the personal debt burden. A sensitivity test showed that, if interest rates rose by 300 basis points with other conditions unchanged, the index could increase markedly to 67.3 within four quarters.48 Banks should remain vigilant against the risks associated with the continued increase in the personal debt burden. Chart 5.12 Average loan-to-value ratio of new mortgages and personal debt burden Chart 5.13 New mortgages of surveyed authorized institutions The pace of US interest rate hikes remained a major factor affecting the credit risk of corporate loans. However, the actual impact on an individual bank’s asset quality would depend on the characteristics of its corporate loan portfolio. In particular, our assessment based on the accounting data of Hong Kong-listed non-financial corporates found that the trends in the leverage ratios of local and non-local corporates had diverged markedly since the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates being more vulnerable to debt-servicing difficulties.50 Banks should assess the impact of interest rate hikes on the credit risk of loans to non-local corporates. Specifically, corporate leverage, as measured by the weighted average debt-to-equity ratio, increased after the global financial crisis, driven mainly by non-local corporates. The leverage ratio of non-local corporates rose to 85% in the first half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.14), while that of local corporates remained broadly stable. As markets reassessed US inflation risks, global financial markets saw renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their end-January highs, completely reversing their significant gains at the beginning of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rise in global equity markets amid low volatility over the past two years was underpinned by market expectations that the economic environment would remain in a sweet spot of solid growth and low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations are being challenged by the risks of tightened global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionist sentiment and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. Following a modest slowdown around the middle of last year, both housing price growth and transaction volume picked up in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may increase the volatility of fund flows in Hong Kong. Given uncertainties in financial markets, the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant to the risks of greater interest rate volatility and potential fund outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) had hovered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets saw renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their end-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index at one point dropping by more than 10%, completely reversing the significant gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was caused by signs that the global economic recovery might put pressure on persistently low US wages and prices, potentially prompting the US Fed to accelerate its pace of interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global equity markets over the past two years was based on market expectations that economic conditions would remain in a sweet spot. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen, with a synchronised pick-up in economic activities across advanced and emerging market economies. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and personal tax rules, raising market expectations that the strong US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite stronger activities, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with the US equity market in particular repeatedly reaching record highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. Following the short-lived financial market volatility, the risk of tightened global monetary conditions may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its potential output, and the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, prompting the US Fed to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Meanwhile, as the tax cuts will lead to a wider fiscal deficit, the US may issue more government debt in the future, which is expected to add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the US Fed continues to advance its balance sheet normalisation. Outside the US, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect their central banks to scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also cloud the outlook for global economic growth. The US Government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns over whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and heighten global financial market volatility. Given the above uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, the sustainability of the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets is in question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical growth in global demand and the expected increase in the fiscal deficit resulting from US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R\*); together with the expected rise in the term premium arising from the US Fed’s balance sheet normalisation, this may push up long-term interest rates and weigh on asset market valuations. In East Asia, the regional economies also enjoyed a sweet spot of solid growth and moderate inflation. Alongside strong economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows accelerated and financial markets rallied. However, the favourable outlook faces downside risks from tightened global liquidity as major central banks synchronously advance monetary policy normalisation; the US Government’s inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and potentially tighter offshore US dollar liquidity arising from large-scale profit repatriation by US corporations in response to the one-off “deemed repatriation” provision under the US tax reform. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of capital flows, with highly leveraged sectors and economies most vulnerable to tightened financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by solid consumption, strong infrastructure investment and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. Meanwhile, signs of the emergence of the “new economy” became increasingly evident, with sectors such as high value-added manufacturing and services displaying strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term economic growth outlook remains positive, although uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the “new economy” can help offset the near-term pressure on growth from further structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, especially in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks’ exposures to corporates in industries with overcapacity remained contained, while shadow banking activities also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capability appear to have tightened, possibly because of reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017 amid stabilising economic conditions and receding risks. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for 2017 as a whole, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow solidly in the second half of 2017. Aggregate investment spending also rebounded on the back of increased corporate capital spending. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports continuing to support growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government and the market consensus forecast real GDP growth of 3–4% and 3.0% respectively for 2018. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, Mainland China’s economic performance amid tightened financial conditions, and developments in local asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a nearly 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained contained. However, quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum showed signs of picking up slightly in recent months, with prices of both tradable goods and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up to a level that remains moderate, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of increases in newly contracted private housing rentals. Driven by funding demand from initial public offerings and seasonal funding demand, tighter liquidity conditions and increased unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities revived, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017. In early 2018, the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable despite turbulence in global financial markets, particularly equity markets. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered. HIBORs came under upward pressure between September and December 2017. This mainly reflected funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management towards the year end. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively from six months earlier to 0.25% and 1.26%. After edging down in early January 2018, HIBORs remained broadly stable and were unaffected by the recent global financial market correction. Despite intense competition in mortgage lending, banks’ average lending rate for new mortgages followed the rise in short-term HIBORs and increased to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, retail banks’ cost of funding remained generally low after a brief increase in October due to initial public offering activities, with the composite interest rate standing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure; a sharp shift in global financial market sentiment could also increase fund-flow volatility. For 2017 as a whole, total bank loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following strong growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. In particular, growth in domestic loans to most sectors and loans for use outside Hong Kong both decelerated. Growth in foreign currency loans slowed, partly due to higher US dollar funding costs. By contrast, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly amid a favourable domestic economic environment and the relatively low cost of Hong Kong dollar funding. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio rose in the second half of 2017 to 82.7% at the year end, the highest level since March 2015. On the other hand, reflecting the relatively slow growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency LTD ratio declined to 63.1% at the year end. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool (comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) edged up in the second half after a modest decline in the first half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decline, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong picked up in the second half. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continuing internationalisation of the renminbi.

The momentum of synchronised strengthening in the global economy since late 2016 showed no signs of abating. Improved growth prospects drove global equity markets steadily higher in 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking the end of the calm conditions in financial markets over the previous two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tightened global financial conditions and a range of policy and event risks will continue to cloud the global outlook. Against the backdrop of a tight labour market, US tax cuts may accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Fed continues to advance balance sheet normalisation, increased issuance of US Treasury securities to finance the tax cuts may add to upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The spectre of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent recovery in global trade. In East Asia, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017, supported by robust export performance and stable domestic demand. However, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it is also subject to various downside risks, such as potentially greater-than-expected tightening in global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies and geopolitical tensions. The materialisation of these downside risks would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges, as they must guard against risks to economic growth while limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance-sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. Some progress was made during the review period in structural reforms and containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remained positive but was still subject to uncertainties, partly depending on the extent to which the rapid growth of the “new economy” could offset the near-term pressure on growth arising from further advancement of structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks receded, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. With the momentum of the cyclical economic improvement becoming increasingly entrenched since late 2016, growth in advanced and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, investment and exports in the US increased solidly, supported by improved private-sector optimism and a significant depreciation of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports of emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilisation of global commodity prices and stronger import demand from the major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In view of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real gross domestic product growth forecasts As growth momentum strengthened in the Euro area and Japan, market expectations that divergence in global monetary policy would narrow, together with more optimistic global growth prospects, boosted risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite three rate hikes by the Fed during the year and the commencement of balance sheet normalisation, the US dollar index still declined by nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite a broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in the major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks’ targets, leading markets until recently to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly reaching record highs and pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the “dot-com bubble” in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would increase the fiscal deficit and inflation had driven US long-term Treasury yields steadily higher, casting doubt on the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. After US average hourly earnings growth for January 2018 came in higher than expected, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index at one point fell by more than 10% from its 26 January high, completely erasing its significant gains at the start of the year, and remained under pressure after the US Government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index at one point soaring to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the narrow-range volatility environment that had persisted over the previous two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, beyond short-term equity market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to US long-term bond yields and possible monetary policy tightening by other major central banks may all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, thereby clouding the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform included certain provisions expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures under the tax reform included: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investment, and (3) a one-off “deemed repatriation” provision that would help reduce incentives for US corporations to retain their overseas profits abroad. Although it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its potential output, the tax cuts may push US output beyond its potential, leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise by more than expected, the Fed may be prompted to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. The federal funds rate path currently expected by financial markets is flatter than the forecasts published by the Fed. However, if inflation rebounds unexpectedly, the risk of an abrupt repricing of rate-hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate forecasts Second, given that the tax reform may exacerbate the fiscal deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase in the future. As the Fed continues to implement its balance sheet normalisation programme, the term premium is expected to rise; under these circumstances, increased US Treasury issuance may intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. In addition, as market expectations of the passage of the US tax-cut package increased, US inflation expectations had risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Accordingly, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield had risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased Treasury supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-year, 5-year forward inflation expectations In addition, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R\*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for an extended period as widely expected. Although estimates of R\* vary, it is generally believed to have fallen substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, US R\* may face upside risks in the future because (1) the expected increase in the fiscal deficit would reduce the national saving rate, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure may raise the investment rate. A rise in R\*, together with the expected increase in the term premium resulting from the Fed’s balance sheet normalisation, may signal higher long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R\* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, stronger growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan led markets to expect their central banks to scale back monetary accommodation. If this materialises, it may signal synchronised tightening in global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies recorded a broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7).
