In Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real gross domestic product recording an eighth consecutive quarter of positive growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continued to signal accommodative monetary policy amid subdued inflation, brighter economic growth prospects in Europe and Japan (and the continued tightening of Japan’s labour market) led some market participants to expect a further scaling-back of their quantitative easing programmes in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real gross domestic product in selected Euro area member economies Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also threaten the nascent recovery in global economic growth and trade. The US Government appeared increasingly inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, with recent examples including the announcement in January 2018 of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines, and the announcement in early March of import tariffs on steel and aluminium, raising concerns over possible retaliatory measures by its trading partners. Meanwhile, negotiations between the United Kingdom and other European Union countries over post-Brexit trade arrangements were under way and subject to multiple uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade frictions, they may impede global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions, such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East and latent risks of terrorist attacks, may increase global financial market volatility. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a robust note. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main growth driver, while domestic demand also provided stable support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China and a rebound in global demand for technology products all supported the region’s exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressures remained subdued. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated due to lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, owing to slow wage growth in several economies, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained low. Chart 2.9 East Asia: headline and core consumer price inflation\* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a range of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and central banks. The improving economy, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, led to significant increases in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Capital inflows into regional markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total gross portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose with the markets. Indeed, credit risk compensation in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

Hong Kong’s economy maintained solid growth momentum in the second half of 2017 amid buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. Hong Kong’s economic outlook is still subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while local inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks remain. Hong Kong’s economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter on quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was solid, supported by favourable employment and income conditions, still-upbeat consumer sentiment, and positive wealth effects from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activities weakened, higher corporate capital spending led aggregate investment spending to rise visibly in the final quarter after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to weigh on GDP growth, while net exports of services contributed positively to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Sustained economic growth momentum led to an increase in jobs in the second half of 2017. Total employment increased by about 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million, with the most visible increases in the construction, financing and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. As real GDP growth outpaced total employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance will continue to benefit from the improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly on the back of favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar (HKD) interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage debt-servicing burdens on private consumption. Regarding domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. While the improved economic environment will stimulate corporate capital spending, possible interest rate increases may have an adverse impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3% to 4% in 2018, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including those relating to the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, the performance of the Mainland Chinese economy amid tightened financial conditions, and movements in Hong Kong’s asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although month-on-month inflation momentum showed signs of edging up in recent months. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index increased by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The rebound in newly contracted private housing rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and salary per capita As global inflation remains moderate and increases in local costs are stable, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effect of growth in newly contracted private housing rentals. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2018 is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, larger-than-expected increases in global inflation or commodity prices could add to local inflation momentum. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a significant tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the low-interest-rate environment after the 2008 global financial crisis, Hong Kong households’ mortgage indebtedness increased. As the normalisation of US dollar interest rates progresses, Hong Kong dollar (HKD) interest rates will eventually follow US dollar interest rates upwards, correspondingly increasing households’ mortgage debt-servicing burdens in the future and weighing on household consumption. This Box therefore examines the impact of an increase in mortgage debt-servicing burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage debt-servicing burden refers to mortgage debt-servicing payments (i.e. interest payments plus loan principal repayments) as a percentage of income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage debt-servicing burden in transmitting interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution and income effects commonly cited in economic theory, as well as the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices, where there is a mortgage debt-servicing burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and hence household disposable income. This impact will increase with the amount of outstanding housing loans. In addition, loan principal repayments change with the amount of outstanding housing loans, which also affects private consumption by changing household disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption, we estimate the outstanding mortgage debt-servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the current mortgage debt-servicing burden indicator, which applies only to new mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the household sector, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard fixed-instalment formula: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), while rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding housing loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage debt-servicing burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt-servicing burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows estimates of the OMDSR from 1985 to 2017 and the median mortgage payment and loan repayment-to-income ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial Population Census. Both ratios trended downwards in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in aggregate household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the housing market bubble in 1997 and the visible fall in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite the visible rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, as the HKMA’s macro-prudential measures on banks’ housing loans restrained aggregate household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of maturities for new mortgages also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median mortgage payment and loan repayment-to-income ratio We also compare the OMDSR with banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which is the actual debt servicing ratio (DSR) of banks’ new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks’ debt-servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As property prices were lower when existing mortgages were originated, their payments are correspondingly lower than those on new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage debt-servicing burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the debt-servicing burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. banks’ debt-servicing ratio). In addition, banks’ debt-servicing ratio is higher because, in compliance with the HKMA’s prudential supervisory requirements, banks include repayments of non-mortgage loans when calculating the debt-servicing ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly because the HKMA’s prudential supervision of housing loans capped banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which also helped smooth the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio for new mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt-servicing burden indicators, but it is more timely and captures the burden of all outstanding mortgage debt rather than only that of new mortgage debt. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage debt-servicing burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In the short-run equation, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by average real private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we use real income (proxied by median household income, deflated by the composite consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, deflated by the composite consumer price index), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total loans continued to increase in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Fund-flow volatility may increase if sentiment in global financial markets shifts abruptly. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly and stayed around 7.80 from September to November 2017. This mainly reflected increased funding demand from initial public offering activities and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end, which tightened liquidity conditions, in turn slowing interest-rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for US dollars increased, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Moving into 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in an orderly manner. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Indicators of fund flows The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently came under greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index (REER), the Hong Kong dollar REER continued to closely track movements in the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Non-residents’ portfolio investment recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that equity investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting the improved regional economic outlook and upbeat market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents’ debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows from residents’ debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017 amid market optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data indicated that equity investment continued to record inflows despite corrections in global financial markets, while bond investment recorded slight fund outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalisation continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Meanwhile, given the uncertain pace of US monetary policy normalisation and rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board arrangements. Despite the US Fed’s interest rate hikes and continued balance-sheet reduction, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and more recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the CUs were not triggered, the combined total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained broadly unchanged at around HK$1,226.8 billion in the second half. Within the total, the Aggregate Balance decreased, while outstanding EFBNs increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills totalling HK$80 billion to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Moving into 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite the equity market correction. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply increased further in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Within the total, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly because buoyant asset markets increased investment demand. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), but was weighed down by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its asset counterparts On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, growth in US dollar deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, after declining continuously for more than two years, other foreign currency deposits rebounded markedly by 8.4% in the second half. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in renminbi deposits. As growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offering activities and banks’ cautious approach to liquidity management ahead of month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December on a monthly average basis. The negative spreads between one- to three-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly mirroring movements in the US dollar yield curve. During the second half, the yield on the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on the ten-year Hong Kong Government Bond increased by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Moving into 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, HIBORs declined in early January. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, HIBORs remained broadly stable. The overnight and three-month HIBORs closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. On the retail front, although banks’ lending rates rose alongside the surge in HIBORs, banks’ cost of funding generally remained low because of the still-large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks’ average lending rate for new mortgages gradually increased by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in the one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, although the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, rose briefly in October amid increased funding demand from initial public offering activities, it remained soft for most of the second half and closed at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise and other major economies may begin normalising interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Meanwhile, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase fund-flow volatility. Nevertheless, the sizeable Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can serve as a buffer to help moderate excessively rapid increases in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to discounting through the Discount Window will also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth reached 10.2% in the first half before slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analysed by currency, supported by favourable domestic economic conditions and the relatively low cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Within the latter, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly because of the rising cost of US dollar funding. For 2017 as a whole, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong, including trade finance, declined from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major industries (Chart 4.11). Growth in loans for building and construction, property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because banks had been required to strengthen risk management of lending to property developers since June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade finance and transport recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail trades declined. By contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related companies remained strong, partly reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans to selected industries Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and other loans for personal purposes, accelerated further to 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management customers secured by financial assets. Growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such secured loans were manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidance to banks in January 2014 on risk management for personal loans, requiring them to adopt prudent risk management measures, including caps on loan tenors and borrowers’ debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, despite increased residential transaction volumes, the loan-to-value ratio of newly approved mortgages declined, and growth in residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household debt to GDP increased from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Mainly benefiting from growth in net interest income, retail banks’ profit improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Credit growth moderated in the second half of 2017 following strong growth in the first half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a notable rise in Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar (HKD) funding costs remained low because of low retail deposit rates. Nevertheless, banks should remain vigilant against the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential fund outflows amid US monetary policy normalisation, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued increase in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality if interest rates rise more than expected. To strengthen banks’ resilience to systemic risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer ratio will be raised to 2.5% from 1 January 2019. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 13.6% in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a decrease in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as assets grew faster than profits, retail banks’ return on assets edged down to 1.15% in the second half of 2017 from 1.17% in the first half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 was still higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 15.8%, while their return on assets rose to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.2). Anecdotal evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margin was consistent with the increase in the average spread on HKD corporate loans in Hong Kong’s syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread on HKD syndicated loans Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose across the board from September 2017, mainly because of liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and banks’ year-end liquidity needs, as well as expectations of US interest rate increases. In particular, the 3-month HIBOR reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up by 53 basis points from the end of June, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, HIBORs appeared to have stabilised as banks’ year-end liquidity demand subsided. Despite the recent increases in HIBORs, retail banks’ HKD funding costs remained stable. This was mainly attributable to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, stayed low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was observed in the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 35 basis points, while average deposit funding costs edged up by 12 basis points. Overall, licensed banks’ average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs increased by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The increase in HIBORs exceeded that in the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking system, which may help improve the interest margin on banks’ assets benchmarked against HIBORs. However, this improvement may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have reduced the spreads between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates, or introduced fixed-rate mortgage plans to attract new customers. With further US interest rate increases expected this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Given intense competition in the loan market, banks’ net interest margins may come under pressure if higher funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be well-capitalised. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently issued a consultation paper on proposed rules prescribing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing authorized institutions’ loss-absorbing capacity would benefit society by helping reduce the likelihood of financial crises, it would inevitably entail costs. Box 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. The liquidity positions of the banking system, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) of category 1 institutions rose to 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 144.2% in the second quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions edged down to 49.4% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 49.7% in the second quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions indicates that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks’ medium- to long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficiently stable funding sources for their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the main funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system’s stable funding structure. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The HKD loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all authorized institutions rose to 82.7% at the end of December 2017 from 77.1% at the end of June (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in HKD loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign-currency LTD ratio declined to 63.1% at the end of December 2017 from 65.5% at the end of June. Overall, the all-currency LTD ratio rose to 73.0% from 71.4% six months earlier. Banks should assess the implications of the rising LTD ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, we estimate that the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would decrease by an amount equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue raising interest rates and normalising its balance sheet, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate but still favourable economic environment, growth in the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions moderated to 5.3% from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half. After two years of moderating growth, total loans grew solidly by 16.1% in 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross classified loan ratio (CLR) and the overdue and rescheduled loans ratio of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loans ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risks. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks As banks became more optimistic about near-term credit growth, strong credit growth was expected to continue. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2017 showed that 29% of surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase in the next 3 months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). The credit risk of personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks’ housing loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value ratio for newly approved housing loans declined further to 48.8% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 50.1% in the second quarter (Chart 5.12). This loan-to-value ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA implemented its first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures, namely in September 2009.

The global economy continued to grow, but momentum weakened amid increased uncertainties arising from ongoing trade frictions, tightened financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The US Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, stressing that its decisions would be “data dependent” and that “patience” was needed, leading investors to rule out the possibility of further interest rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) triggered the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, HKD trading continued in a smooth and orderly manner. Total loan growth moderated slightly in the second half of 2018, reflecting reduced credit demand amid headwinds including the ongoing US-China trade conflicts and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes falling markedly and housing prices declining, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds from increased uncertainties in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, they could significantly dampen business sentiment and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profitability. Given the continued increase in corporate leverage, banks should carefully assess the impact that a possible deterioration in the external environment could have on the credit risk of their relevant corporate loans. The global economy continued to grow in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy grew solidly, growth momentum slowed elsewhere. Among advanced economies, growth slowed and inflation remained low in Japan and several major euro area countries. Slowing global trade and a marked decline in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of weakening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund in January lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively from its October 2018 projections. Global equity markets experienced substantial volatility towards the end of 2018 amid a dimmer growth outlook and escalating trade frictions. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, raising market concerns that the US was heading towards a recession. Nevertheless, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and a recession in the near term was unlikely. Even so, the global economic outlook remained fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation gave the US Fed room to pause its interest rate hikes, its data-dependent policy bias also suggested that financial markets might become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of US-China and US-EU trade negotiations remained uncertain. In the UK, it was still unclear whether a solution to avert a “hard Brexit” could be achieved. In East Asia, financial markets stabilised as the US dollar’s appreciation slowed and markets expected the US Fed to pause its interest rate hikes, but a deterioration in the external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade growth momentum had already weighed on economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures had also eased. Although this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks in balancing support for growth against curbing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector indebtedness in some economies in the region remained severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia was that an unexpected change in the US Fed’s monetary policy could cause shocks that spill over to the sovereign debt markets of emerging market economies, including East Asian economies. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 amid increased uncertainties in the external environment and a modest slowdown in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remained uncertain as the US-China trade negotiations had yet to reach a conclusion. A marked contraction in shadow financing activities had increased financing difficulties for private enterprises, especially small firms, over the past few quarters, while weakening economic confidence could also put pressure on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers needed to continue balancing economic stabilisation against the prevention and containment of potential systemic risks through accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted cuts in reserve requirement ratios. Meanwhile, the authorities also adopted more supply-side measures to enhance productivity growth, such as promoting competition among firms under different forms of ownership, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0%–6.5%. Risk-off sentiment dominated Mainland financial markets in 2018. Banks’ asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage of listed non-financial firms increased modestly. However, banks’ loan impairment charges increased further in the second half of 2018, while their exposures to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline, with both developments helping to protect the banking system against a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage of listed firms in industries with excess capacity—one of the major sources of bank credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors behind the recent improvement in the business performance of industries with excess capacity. Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half. Sequential GDP growth stalled and year-on-year growth also slowed, bringing full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activity was mainly attributable to consumption and exports being weighed down directly or indirectly by the US-China trade conflicts. Slower private consumption growth might reflect increased economic uncertainties and negative wealth effects from the correction in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports also deteriorated, particularly after the US and China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the US-China trade conflicts on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and explores the near-term outlook and associated risks. Mainly due to slower global economic growth, economic growth was expected to moderate further in 2019. Amid the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance was expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption was expected to continue supporting economic growth amid a low unemployment rate and rising household income, but the outlook for aggregate investment could become more uncertain. The Government forecast real GDP growth of 2%–3% in 2019, while private-sector analysts’ latest growth forecasts averaged 2.3%. These forecasts were subject to the various uncertainties and risks described above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight increase in inflation partly reflected earlier growth in rentals for newly leased private residential properties. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years, growth in total employment showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures were expected to remain moderate in 2019 as domestic economic growth momentum weakened. After the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and traded between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered another four times in March 2019 (up to 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate appreciated in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar depreciated against the US dollar, partly due to the rebuilding of carry trade positions. Despite the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered again in March, HKD trading continued in a smooth and orderly manner. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as at 19 March). Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally increased in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the three-month and 12-month HIBORs each rose by around 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December on a monthly average basis. Entering 2019, HIBORs generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average cost of HKD funding, increased from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. In view of the increased cost of funding, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in late September. At the end of January 2019, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose in tandem with the Best Lending Rates to around 2.45%. As uncertainties related to US-China trade frictions and the Brexit negotiations persisted, volatility in fund flows could intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates could spur arbitrage activities and lead to fund outflows. Under these circumstances, fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi exchange rates had faced depreciation pressures amid market concerns over escalating US-China trade frictions. However, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November on optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between the US and China. Despite the continued US-China trade frictions, funding conditions in the offshore interbank market had not been significantly affected thus far. Overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half, with renminbi customer deposits increasing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite concerns over US-China trade frictions, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to continue expanding with Mainland’s capital account liberalisation, the development of Stock Connect and Bond Connect, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. The local equity market experienced a roller-coaster ride over the past six months. In the early part of the review period, the market declined sharply amid continued US monetary policy tightening, major differences between the two sides in the US-China trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in Mainland China. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the US Fed shifted to a “patient” monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade-war truce, China took further measures to reduce its net trade with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the US brought a highly politicised legal prosecution against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides made conciliatory gestures signalling their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local equity market rebounded sharply at the beginning of the year. However, considerable uncertainty remained as the two sides discussed the details of any agreement, while future developments in the US federal prosecution would complicate the situation, particularly in the high-technology sector. The HKD debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, while performance improved towards year-end as market expectations of a slower pace of US monetary policy normalisation strengthened. As a result, fund flows into bond funds reversed course and increased modestly in the second half. Issuance in Hong Kong’s CNH market rebounded sharply after three consecutive years of decline. However, as Mainland firms continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remained challenging, with its outlook dependent on global economic developments, particularly those in Mainland China.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened under the combined effects of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly outside the US. In view of the dimmer growth outlook, the Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be “data dependent” and require “patience”, and no longer provided forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. As the Fed’s policy stance becomes data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data and may perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. At the same time, heightened global trade policy uncertainties and geopolitical risks may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since end-2018 amid signs of a slowdown in the US rate-hike cycle and a stabilising US dollar. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown due to a deteriorating external environment, namely the unresolved China-US trade conflicts and weaker growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth momentum moderated further in the second half of 2018, while uncertainties surrounding the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflicts and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Policymakers therefore introduced more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. In the face of these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and control systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow broadly. However, while the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of moderation emerged. There were also clear signs of weakening growth momentum outside the US. A number of country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian government bond yields amid a fiscal stand-off with the European Union, and social unrest in France, weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth weighed on industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp decline in oil prices in the fourth quarter also posed new challenges to commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for global growth in 2019 by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices of selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production in emerging market economies In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent a sharp correction amid weakening global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainties, market concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the Fed’s remarks that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry that a US recession was imminent (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Treasury yields and probability of a US recession Nevertheless, the likelihood of a US recession in the near term is low. US economic fundamentals remain robust, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, and the likelihood of economic overheating prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy substantially is low. However, possibly taking into account the substantial tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data dependent and noted that moderate inflationary pressures allowed them to be “patient” in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the US Federal Open Market Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes and announced that it “would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments”. This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World ex-US Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Fed’s recent “dovish” signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain and depends on inflation and other developments. Moderate inflationary pressures to date have given the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary normalisation. Stable inflation expectations in recent years support the view that it “can afford to be patient” (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chairman Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slower growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainties. In view of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations However, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting the overall performance of the US economy. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which usually implies that inflation could intensify in the future (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that have largely ruled out the possibility of a Fed rate hike in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds target range remaining unchanged and of at least one rate hike in 2019 Overall, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data dependent as a risk-management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the Euro area, the European Central Bank ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the European Central Bank downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, describing the risks surrounding the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside”. The implications of this downgrade to its economic growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan stated at its latest policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary easing could be considerable, as its effectiveness has been questioned and the drawbacks of a prolonged ultra-low interest rate environment have become increasingly evident. For example, regional banks’ capital ratios fell from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from uncertainties relating to the global monetary policy outlook, uncertain outcomes of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two other major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. In early December, the US Government announced that it would not increase tariffs on imports from China for 90 days, and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the US and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. The uncertain outcomes of these trade negotiations may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the US, disagreements between the two parties over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives may lead to further policy gridlock in the future. In the UK, risks relating to Brexit and its spillovers surged after the May government’s Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and whether a plan can be devised at the last minute to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit” remains uncertain. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the renewed US sanctions on Iran, may also create uncertainties for oil prices and thereby affect global growth prospects. In East Asia, after fluctuating during the first three quarters of last year, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter. The stabilisation of the US dollar since October and signs that the Fed would be patient about further rate hikes eased the currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures facing East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to a net inflow (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: currency index and capital flows Despite financial market stability, there are growing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflicts weakened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real gross domestic product growth in most East Asian economies to moderate in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies, which reflect near-term external trade performance, have fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that near-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers’ Index new export orders indices for East Asian economies Amid slowing growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: headline inflation rate and oil prices As recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar have both been moderate, East Asian central banks no longer face an urgent need to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy dilemma of balancing economic growth against containing inflation and capital outflows. However, as private-sector indebtedness in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

Hong Kong’s economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weaker export performance amid the US-China trade dispute. With global growth slowing, real GDP growth is also expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy and the performance of the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019, while the outlook is subject to potential upside and downside risks. Hong Kong’s economic activities softened in the second half of 2018. In particular, economic activities failed to maintain the strong momentum seen in the first half, with quarter-on-quarter GDP growth turning slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Year on year, economic growth also moderated, with growth in the fourth quarter at 1.3%, below trend growth, dragging down full-year growth from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Based on the expenditure-based, seasonally adjusted GDP volume index. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component The weakening in economic activities was mainly attributable to drags on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect effects of the US-China trade conflicts. Growth in private consumption moderated, possibly due to increased economic uncertainties and negative wealth effects arising from corrections in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Aggregate investment spending declined visibly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after the US and China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 takes a closer look at Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms As economic activities weakened, job growth appeared to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to about 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, less than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. With weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly flat, with no signs of significant improvement. As global economic growth slows further, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Against a challenging external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, while the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, growth in private consumption is expected to moderate, partly due to weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effects arising from earlier corrections in asset prices. For fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily alongside increased housing supply, firms may become more cautious about capital investment as economic uncertainties increase. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index continued to hover in contractionary territory, and forecasts of future economic growth based on the index point to a further moderation in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2 and 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts by private-sector analysts range from 1.5 to 2.7%. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to the various risks and uncertainties discussed in the previous two chapters. Although local inflationary pressures continued to build up in recent months, they remained moderate. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight rise in inflation momentum was driven by increases in certain services prices. Earlier growth in newly contracted private housing rentals and faster increases in the prices of meals bought away from home continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures remained broadly moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita payroll Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019. This mainly reflects weaker domestic growth momentum. However, the earlier increases in private housing rentals will continue to pass through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecast for the full-year headline inflation rate is a moderate 2.2%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, the lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the currently near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if the US-China trade frictions ease and the local economy performs better than expected, local inflation could be pushed up. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The US-China trade conflicts intensified progressively in the second half of 2018: on July 6 and August 23, the US imposed additional tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China respectively. Immediately following these two measures, Mainland China responded by imposing additional tariffs of 25% on an equivalent value of US goods. The US stepped up its measures further on September 24 by imposing additional tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China promptly responded by imposing additional tariffs of 5 to 10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. The two countries have since entered into negotiations to avoid further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the additional tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The US-China trade dispute therefore has important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify traded goods directly affected by the additional tariffs, thereby taking a closer look at their impact. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extract data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports affected by the successive rounds of additional tariffs described in the previous section. In the first two rounds, the US imposed tariffs mainly on capital goods and semi-finished goods, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods was broadened to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of additional tariffs as List 1, List 2 and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus on analysing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. In addition, caution is warranted when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activities in that month were disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analytical results in this section should only be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of the additional tariffs. Hong Kong re-exports of tariff-affected goods originating from the Mainland Shortly after the additional tariffs were imposed, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US appeared to have declined significantly or registered slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the additional tariffs were imposed, while re-exports of List 3 recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports of all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US in 2018 Hong Kong re-exports of tariff-affected goods originating from the US By comparison, goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports of List 1 appeared to have declined significantly in the few months after the additional tariffs were imposed, but rebounded towards the end of the year. Re-exports of List 2 recorded broadly negative growth throughout the year, while growth in List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018 Front-loading Since there is sometimes a time lag between the announcement and eventual implementation of tariffs (or simply because of the threat of additional tariffs), firms may increase shipments of affected goods ahead of the expected effective date of the tariffs. Indeed, some information and news reports indicate that such front-loading was quite common. Some private-sector analysts also considered such behaviour to be one reason for the strong overall trade figures before the additional tariffs were imposed. The more granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for goods on certain tariff lists, but this appeared to involve only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Growth in re-exports of List 1 and List 2 increased in the months before their respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, growth in re-exports from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) showed no clear evidence of front-loading by firms. Hong Kong re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the additional tariffs accounted for only about 4 to 5% of the total value of Hong Kong’s re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs should also be examined. We find that re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in the final two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Moreover, the decline in growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) was visibly larger from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in growth of re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs partly reflected broader weakness in external demand. As trade frictions continued to increase uncertainties, global financial conditions tightened and geopolitical risks rose, external demand could come under more widespread pressure. In particular, the trade conflicts have weighed on global economic sentiment and activities, as reflected in corrections in major equity markets. Import demand in other economies was consequently dampened, constraining Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong’s re-exports in 2018 Even if the US-China trade frictions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth may slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is bound to further constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that firms of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trading sector particularly subdued. Other trade-related industries, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Survey of business outlook in Hong Kong’s import and export sector

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades as liquidity tightened in anticipation of seasonal funding demand. Moving into 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly due to corporates repatriating funds raised from IPOs and the market rebuilding carry trade positions, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. HIBORs generally increased in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before declining in January 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar fund flows may become more volatile amid uncertainties arising from the ongoing US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, carry trade activities may continue, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and traded between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again a total of 4 times in March 2019 (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, but then declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again from November onwards as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity, leading to the unwinding of carry trades. Moving into 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates repatriating funds raised from IPOs and the market rebuilding carry trade positions. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, prompting market participants to engage in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, the Hong Kong dollar gradually weakened and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance had remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), before declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March (as of 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar funds that had flowed out since April 2018 accounted for only a small portion of the approximately HK$1 trillion inflows since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund-flow indicators Broadly tracking movements of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and therefore had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER The latest balance of payments statistics indicated that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and heightened equity market volatility, outflows of local residents’ equity securities investment accelerated, more than offsetting inflows of non-residents’ portfolio investment in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both local residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, fund-flow volatility may intensify amid uncertainties arising from the ongoing US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities and lead to fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are both part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation and the repeated triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half to HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4).
