The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which reduced the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base Regarding the broader measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. The broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) increased by 3.6% in the first half, but only slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits were little changed compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit rates increased. The counterpart analysis showed that the slowdown in Hong Kong dollar M3 growth was attributable to changes in banks’ capital and reserves (included under “net other items”). Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterparts Growth in foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half. As banks attracted more deposits after raising preferential US dollar deposit rates, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half and thus became the main driver of growth in foreign currency deposits (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to grow. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions increased moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Despite the still sizeable Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposits, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank rates, making them more volatile than longer-term interbank rates (Chart 4.7). The three-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, around 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Moving into 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The average three-month and 12-month HIBORs fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, the yields of 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar cost of funding, increased slightly. Reflecting changes in the costs of interbank and deposit funding, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before falling to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of the higher cost of funding, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September. However, retail banks did not adjust their Best Lending Rates again after the target range for the US federal funds rate was raised once more in December. Meanwhile, the average lending rate for new mortgages increased in tandem with the Best Lending Rates, reaching around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, movements in US dollar interest rates, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as IPO subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains sizeable and the banking system holds a large amount of Exchange Fund Bills, which banks can use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating US-China trade tensions, both offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar from the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, amid optimism generated by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US, both CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore renminbi and CNH was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates So far, the ongoing US-China trade tensions have not had a material impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting the monetary easing measures recently introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of developments in the US-China trade negotiations on liquidity in the CNH interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Within these deposits, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, outstanding certificates of deposit declined further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to lower issuance of certificates of deposit and the relatively large amount of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Mainly benefiting from an increase in net interest income, retail banks’ profitability continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressures on Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, retail banks’ overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs increased notably, but remained at relatively low levels. Amid uncertainties in the external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation since November, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from persistent uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations, the global economic slowdown, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued increase in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant to the impact that a possible further deterioration in the external environment may have on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while their return on assets rose to 1.23% from 1.14% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly attributable to substantial growth in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 19.4%, while their return on assets rose to 1.27% from 1.16% in 2017. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Retail banks’ net interest margin widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period a year earlier (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Broadly reflecting further US interest rate hikes and a decline in Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the interbank market following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong dollar interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period, as banks generally raised time deposit rates to compete for longer-term stable funding. In addition, following the US interest rate hike decision in late September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Reflecting increases in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) rose to 0.89% in December from 0.62% in June 2018, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upwards. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs increased by 36 basis points, following an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The cumulative increase in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates exceeded the rise in banks’ overall funding costs in Hong Kong, which may have had a positive impact on retail banks’ housing loans benchmarked against Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates, a type of loan actively promoted by the industry in recent years. However, further improvement in net interest margins may become more limited, as most housing loans benchmarked against Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates have already reached their Best Lending Rate-based caps. As the timing of future increases in Best Lending Rates remains uncertain, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation may weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, heightened uncertainties in the external environment may cloud banks’ earnings outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, persistent uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations may dampen business sentiment and reduce demand for bank credit. If this results in a significant decline in lending and deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks’ profitability. The Hong Kong banking sector remained strongly capitalised, well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions increased further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Since 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions have been required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based Leverage Ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum Leverage Ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) of category 1 institutions rose to 167.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 from 156.6% in the second quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also rose to 54.3% in the fourth quarter from 51.3% in the second quarter, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated stable funding positions among authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding a range of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2018, customer deposits as a share of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions edged up to 55.7% from 54.5% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all authorized institutions fell to 72.6% at year-end from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions fell to 58.3% from 65.2% over the same period. By contrast, as growth in Hong Kong dollar deposits was much slower than that in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged up to 86.9% at year-end from 85.4% at the end of June 2018. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks decreased slightly in the second half of 2018. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, it is estimated that the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would decrease by an amount equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks 1. The interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard 200-basis-point parallel interest rate shock on institutions’ interest rate risk exposures. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainties surrounding China-US trade conflicts, tightening global financial liquidity and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed markedly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Growth in domestic loans slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, growth in total loans slowed markedly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain subdued in the near term. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2018 showed that, among all surveyed authorized institutions, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next 3 months, while the share of authorized institutions expecting demand to decline rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite a slight decrease in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loans ratio of all authorized institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio declined slightly to 0.50%, while the overdue and rescheduled loans ratio edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks 1. Classified loans refer to loans classified as “substandard”, “doubtful” or “loss”. 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of retail banks’ Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. Since December 2015, the coverage of the figures has been expanded to include retail banks’ major overseas subsidiaries. On a half-yearly basis, growth in loans to individuals slowed to 3.9% in the second half of 2018 from 5.3% in the first half. This was mainly attributable to slower growth in personal loans (including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal GDP grew more slowly than loans to individuals, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up to 71.9% in the fourth quarter of 2018 from 71.2% in the second quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak since early 2020 has hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic shock from the outbreak, financial markets remain volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthening, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable and total deposits growing modestly, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After rebounding modestly in the first half of 2019, total loan growth slowed in the second half. The residential property market generally softened, albeit with some fluctuations, from mid-2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increases in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact of a possible intensification of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth had initially shown signs of stabilisation, benefiting from stepped-up monetary easing by major central banks, the easing of US-China trade tensions and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit”. However, the continued rise in global coronavirus cases since late January has sparked market concerns and triggered substantial volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks posed by the outbreak, several major central banks sharply cut interest rates and expanded their liquidity facilities, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp falls in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will weigh on global economic activity, with the extent of the economic shock depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, tensions between the US and its major trading partners may escalate again, while post-Brexit trade negotiations between the UK and the EU may also prove difficult. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia1. East Asia’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but whether the technology product cycle is experiencing a broad-based rebound remains to be seen. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One US-China trade agreement announced in December 2019, with the trade truce reducing global trade uncertainties to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by several economies in the region may hurt tourism in Asia, particularly in economies that are more dependent on tourism service exports. Given the region’s close supply-chain links with Mainland China, manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One US-China trade agreement has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made economic stability a priority for 2020, while also emphasising the control of financial vulnerabilities. The latest consensus forecast indicates that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private-owned enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts noted that private-owned industrial enterprises might have faced declining shareholders’ equity in recent years, which was viewed as a sign of “private-sector retreat”. Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in the equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed-company data and finds that private-owned enterprises or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. While the study finds that negative earnings are the largest driver, other factors, especially structural factors, also warrant attention (see Box 2 for details). Economic activity in Hong Kong contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weak domestic demand, especially the contraction in private consumption, was the main drag on GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely disrupted consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook that in turn dampened consumer and business sentiment. With renewed escalation in US-China trade tensions, slowing global economic growth and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater scope to step up support for the domestic economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would lower banks’ countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent outbreak also posing significant downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism and transport have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget could provide relief to households and businesses, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% Government guarantee for businesses under the “SME Financing Guarantee Scheme”. 2 The HKMA’s further reduction of banks’ countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks greater scope to step up support for the domestic economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater near-term pressure from the outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment will likely remain weak amid fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One US-China trade agreement is expected to have a modest positive impact on the domestic economy in the near term. 3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-boundary economic activities, such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the growth forecasts of international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks arising from the global economic slowdown, US-China trade relations, Mainland China’s economic performance and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate will rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 discusses recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook in greater detail. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build through the third quarter of 2019, mainly because of higher prices for fresh pork; thereafter, inflation momentum gradually eased as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to moderate in the near term amid weak economic conditions, consolidating private housing rentals and modest imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts for the headline inflation rate in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including demand associated with initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually from mid-October 2019. Moving into December, the strengthening momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate increased further, partly because of buoyant initial public offering activities and partly because tightening liquidity towards year-end prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, and neither of the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) was triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital-market activities such as initial public offerings. Box 4 examines how market interest in future initial public offering activities affects the three-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually increased from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest-rate cap set with reference to the Best Lending Rate, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October. However, as Best Lending Rates in the market were lowered from November, the average lending rate for new mortgages edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthening, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable and total deposits growing modestly, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. Nevertheless, the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus outbreak amid uncertainties in the external environment needs to be monitored. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the ability, resources and determination to deal with fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened amid market expectations of a US-China trade agreement, but faced weakening pressure from the coronavirus outbreak since late January 2020. The offshore renminbi (CNH) generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi in the latter part of 2019. Its discount widened briefly at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool recovered slightly after edging down in the previous review period. At the end of January 2020, outstanding renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion. Hong Kong’s other renminbi businesses also grew, with strong growth recorded in renminbi bank loans and renminbi trade settlement. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion for 2019 as a whole. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased allocations to renminbi assets by international investors, and deeper regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes of a global economic recovery. However, the continued rise in global coronavirus infections since late January 2020 dashed hopes of a recovery and heightened investor concerns about a global recession, triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. In response to the economic shock, major central banks and some governments introduced stimulus measures from early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 clouded the outlook for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak was expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia continued to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the phase-one trade agreement between China and the US helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downside pressures remained amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities’ monetary and fiscal policy responses would provide some cushion. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, continued weakness in manufacturing and investment left global economic growth lacklustre in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed tentative signs of stabilisation in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier easing measures of the US Fed and the ECB, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US “phase-one” trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index However, the continued rise in global coronavirus infections since late January and the ensuing economic shock raised market concerns and triggered a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays an important role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activity in the Mainland and the resulting drag on its economic growth would generate significant spillovers that could potentially spread worldwide (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infections outside Mainland China could intensify supply-chain disruptions and pose a risk of directly weighing on local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and option-adjusted spread of the Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) In response to the potentially severe economic shock from the epidemic, some central banks, including the US Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, cut interest rates from early March, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nevertheless, financial markets remained under immense selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening in global financial conditions, which could in turn exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index Apart from the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also clouded the global economic outlook. In particular, although policy risks surrounding trade tensions declined following the China-US phase-one trade agreement, subsequent negotiations could be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remained unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK were not expected to proceed smoothly, prolonging post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March would put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019 amid sluggish global demand. The region’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there were tentative signs that the downturn in the regional technology-product cycle was bottoming out, including reports by major electronics companies in the region of improved earnings at the end of 2019,6 it remained to be seen whether exports of technology products in the region had staged a solid rebound. Chart 2.5 East Asia: merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital investment declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region’s economic growth potential over the longer term. To support economic growth amid moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and Korea further lowered their policy rates in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak raised concerns that economies in the region could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As a number of economies in the region imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism sector bore the brunt, particularly in economies more dependent on visitors from Mainland China and exports of tourism services (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and worsening epidemic would also affect regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: tourism exports and Chinese tourists In the near term, the epidemic would continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Based on the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these effects could be transient, but the actual outcome would depend on the severity and geographical spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also faced multiple headwinds. First, although corporate earnings were expected to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions encouraged the search for yield, pushing up asset prices without support from fundamentals. As a result, regional equity markets became more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituents of benchmark equity indices Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth could make it more difficult for the region’s private sector to service its debt. Although lower domestic interest rates could provide breathing space for indebted corporations and households, they could also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of debt overhang in the private sector could also increase, although this effect might be confined to longer-term borrowing by corporations with stronger financial fundamentals. Third, on the external front, East Asian economies could face increased risks from an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress on the China-US phase-one trade agreement, China-US trade tensions persisted as the fundamental trade issues between the two countries remained unresolved. The widening net trade surpluses of several regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9) suggested that multinational corporations might continue to seek more sourcing channels outside China-centred supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative net trade surplus of nine emerging market economies in Asia (excluding China) with the US had increased to around US$167 billion. If net trade surpluses with the US continued to widen, the relevant Asian economies could become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed punitive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remained highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise net trade surplus with the US Over the past decade, increased integration of international financial markets led to significant growth in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study found that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows were driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices, commonly known as passive funds, but also actively managed funds that use investment indices as benchmarks.9 By bringing in overseas investors that the economies concerned could not otherwise attract or access, these funds help promote financial market development in emerging market economies. In turn, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor bases, supporting long-term market growth and stability. But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, there are market concerns that investments by such funds could weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby leading to high corporate leverage.10 Moreover, it has been argued that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has increased the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, more vulnerable.11 This Box assesses the implications of index-driven investment for financial stability in relation to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investments to constituent bonds according to their weights in a benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds could reduce the incentive for issuers of index constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour could encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and debt-servicing risks to the corporate sector in emerging market economies, where leverage rose sharply after the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of corporations in each emerging market economy in a major index tracking corporate bonds in emerging market economies as a proxy for passive bond fund investment in their bonds,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term, but not short-term, leverage ratios of the corporate issuers concerned. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated effects. Apart from promoting the development of corporate debt markets in emerging market economies, the broader base of long-term bond investors provided by passive bond funds also benefits corporate development in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effects are significant only for corporations in emerging market economies with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with stronger debt-servicing capacity and lower leverage ratios (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged corporations or those with weaker debt-servicing capacity appear less likely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. Overall, the above study suggests that growth in passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase debt-servicing risks in the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Hong Kong’s economy contracted in the second half of 2019 owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending and subdued export performance, entering its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent coronavirus outbreak posing significant downside risks. The economic outlook is subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate will likely rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. Hong Kong’s economy contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. Year on year, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities slowed visibly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP declined successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main drag on GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, while the weaker economic outlook dampened consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract visibly from the third quarter onwards. 33 Aggregate investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter amid heightened economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment. 34 Externally, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued amid escalating China-US trade tensions, weaker global economic growth and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Chart 3.2). 35 With exports of services contracting sharply, net trade dragged down GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Given the immense headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment and support enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and sectors that had been severely affected, such as retail, food services, transportation and tourism. 36 To give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would lower banks’ countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HKD200 billion to HKD300 billion to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong’s economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent outbreak also posing significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a package of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget could provide relief to households and enterprises, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% Government guarantee for enterprises under the “SME Financing Guarantee Scheme”. 37 The HKMA’s further reduction of banks’ countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy, especially sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressures from the outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment will likely remain weak amid fragile consumer and business sentiment. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a mildly positive impact on the local economy in the near term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-boundary economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the growth forecasts by international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous risks and uncertainties discussed in the preceding chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). In particular, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a nearly ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment declined by 0.5% year on year in the second half of 2019 and continued to fall to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment mainly came from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also declined by 0.3% year on year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Box 3 examines in greater detail the recent developments and near-term outlook of the labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to rising prices of fresh pork; inflation momentum then gradually moderated as economic activities weakened. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index increased by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The moderation in inflation momentum reflected reduced price pressures across a number of consumer price index components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained notable because of rising fresh pork prices, although price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. For services, growth in the consumer price index rental component also trended down as growth in newly contracted private housing rentals moderated earlier (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private housing rentals continue to moderate, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, import inflation is expected to remain moderate owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the headline inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe-than-expected economic deterioration, for example owing to a prolonged coronavirus outbreak, could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, more severe disruptions to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the visible slowdown in Hong Kong’s economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8-2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate rose more visibly to 3.3% at the end of 2019. The labour market will face stronger headwinds in 2020 owing to the coronavirus outbreak. Against this background, this box analyses recent developments and the near-term outlook of the labour market, including why overall labour market conditions remained broadly resilient in the first three quarters of 2019, with little change in the unemployment rate, and the implications for future developments. It also examines some risk factors that could cause the unemployment rate to rise sharply. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labour demand involves costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature explains why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activities deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth and unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade sector and the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors continued to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained sound, while financial activities relating to fintech development and initial public offerings were also highly active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. Moreover, public administration, social and personal services, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appeared to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, public administration, social and personal services respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors even when the economy slows. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, cushioning the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 Meanwhile, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted visibly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, despite the decline in employment during the economic recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped ease pressure on the unemployment rate to rise in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some structural changes in the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the increased share of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the shares of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment have declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, making them the second-largest group in total employment (about 7% in 2017). 42 Companies may therefore retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the larger number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October, with its upward momentum increasing further in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) range in recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly attributable to equity-related demand and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions amid tighter liquidity towards the year end. Overall, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Although coronavirus-induced shifts in market sentiment amid an uncertain external environment may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong, with its sizeable foreign reserves and robust banking system, is able to withstand the pressure of fund outflows without compromising its financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including that arising from initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Moving into December, its upward momentum increased further, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed on the strong side of the CU range from mid-December to February. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant initial public offering activities and partly to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions amid tighter liquidity towards the year end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) Broadly tracking movements of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and thus had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER broadly tracked movements of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER In gauging fund flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong’s banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong’s financial system as a whole. The two fund-flow concepts require different monitoring indicators. In monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, resulting in a weaker Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side CU rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to purchase Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, thereby reducing the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, while the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed on the strong side of the CU range in recent months. Therefore, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar were observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits in Hong Kong’s banking system are a useful indicator. When there are large fund outflows from Hong Kong’s banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a modest pace, indicating that there were no notable cross-border fund outflows. Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner, suggesting that the coronavirus outbreak had so far had only a limited impact on local monetary conditions. Nevertheless, the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak need to be closely monitored. With sizeable foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capacity, resources and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowdown in the local economy, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, increasing by 4.0% from the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As no CU was triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding EFBNs, Certificates of Indebtedness, and Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base Broad measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply remained broadly stable during the review period. Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) increased by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and then edged up by 0.2% during the seven-month period since the end of June 2019. An analysis of counterpart assets indicated that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and an expansion in the Monetary Base (through increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and Government-issued notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). Hong Kong dollar deposits, the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, remained broadly unchanged during the seven-month period since the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to increase modestly, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Foreign currency deposits increased modestly by 2.3% during the seven-month period since the end of June 2019 (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which rose by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, including a slight decrease in renminbi deposits in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) grew steadily by 1.2% from the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s aggregate broad money supply also grew at a relatively steady pace, with aggregate M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively from the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Chart 4.7 Aggregate broad money supply (M2) Although monetary conditions remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, amid buoyant initial public offering activities in the Hong Kong equity market, the overnight HIBOR showed greater volatility on several occasions in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8).44 Other short-term HIBORs generally increased during the review period. Subscriptions for large initial public offerings can exert significant pressure on the overnight HIBOR. The empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to future initial public offering activities also affects the three-month HIBOR. This occurs when market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large initial public offerings and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards along with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond declined by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages On the retail front, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. The increase mainly reflected banks’ continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, which led to an increase in the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of October 2019, several retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, Best Lending Rates of retail banks currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding housing loans, major banks raised the interest rate caps linked to Best Lending Rates for HIBOR-based housing loans, and the average lending rate for new mortgages therefore increased to around 2.63% in October.45 Following the reduction in market Best Lending Rates since November, the average mortgage rate edged down to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although HIBORs track US dollar interest rates in the long run, short-term HIBORs may be affected by local factors that influence demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as initial public offering activities in Hong Kong. Following the decline in the Aggregate Balance of the banking system since April 2018, HIBORs may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funds. However, this does not imply that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet banks’ interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightness, banks can make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid concerns that China-US trade conflicts might intensify, offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened markedly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi (CNH) falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Moving into October, market expectations that China-US trade talks would resume reversed the depreciation trend of the renminbi. CNH and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and once rose above 6.9 in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US. However, since the end of January, both CNH and onshore renminbi have again come under weakening pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. CNH traded at a discount to onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, but generally at a premium later in 2019. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, although the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover between 3-4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR showed brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to MSCI’s A-share adjustments, and around the Lunar New Year holiday at the end of January 2020.

Reflecting increased uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environment, retail banks’ profit in Hong Kong declined slightly in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although growth in total loans moderated in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth over the same period during the review period. Accordingly, both the average all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio and the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio of all authorized institutions (AIs) increased. Nevertheless, given the stable level of the Aggregate Balance of the banking system and broadly stable deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increases in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the potential impact of any intensification of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit59 of retail banks declined slightly by 1.5% in the second half of 2019 compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, from 1.23% in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly to 1.63% in the second half of 2019 from 1.67% in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in retail banks’ loan impairment charges and operating expenses resulted in a slight decline in profit. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three 25-basis-point reductions in the US federal funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has so far not experienced significant downward pressure. Instead, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, affected by a number of domestic factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market. Meanwhile, longer-term HIBORs remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (the blue line in Chart 5.3). On the retail front, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the reduction in US policy rates.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting an increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) gradually increased to 1.09% at the end of 2019 from 0.95% six months earlier, although it remained low by historical standards (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates More broadly, as the decline in US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, their average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of HIBORs, supporting the banking sector’s profit over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding costs and maturities have therefore been calculated as weighted averages of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Accordingly, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and domestic environment will continue to cloud banks’ profitability outlook. These include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future course of China-US trade relations and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could weaken the already subdued momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policy by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, potentially exerting pressure on banks’ future net interest margins. Domestically, the local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to dampen business investment and market confidence. Against an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or intensifies, the outlook for credit demand and banks’ asset quality could deteriorate. In terms of overall market developments, following the granting of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector began rolling out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market shares by launching more convenient products and offering more attractive deposit rates to acquire new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the cost of funding of incumbent banks. Although the near-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks’ operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate their adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results in Box 5 show that the extent of financial technology adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically associated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and well above minimum international standards. At the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated AIs increased further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratios, the Basel III non-risk-based Leverage Ratio requirement is intended to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated AIs The liquidity position of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)65 requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), staying well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also increased moderately to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019 from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019, remaining well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio66, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated stable funding positions among AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the applicable statutory minimum requirement of 75% in 2019. The ample liquidity and stable funding positions of AIs suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand various liquidity shocks. At the end of 2019, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all AIs remained broadly unchanged, edging down to 56.3% from 56.4% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Overall, the average all-currency LTD ratio of all AIs increased to 75.4% at the end of 2019 from 74.5% at the end of June 2019. Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system had remained stable since April 2019 and deposits had remained broadly steady, there were no clear signs of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11).
