Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Amid China-US trade tensions, the global economic slowdown and continuing local social incidents, bank credit growth moderated in the second half of 2019 after rebounding moderately in the first half. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth, as measured by the change in total loans and advances of all AIs, moderated to 2.4% in the second half of 2019 after growing moderately by 4.2% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was attributable to moderating growth during the review period in both domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively, in the second half of 2019, lower than the corresponding increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, growth in total loans for 2019 as a whole increased moderately to 6.7%, from 4.4% in 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines raised hopes of economic reopening and boosted global growth prospects. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets repeatedly reached record highs. However, uncertainties continued to cloud the global outlook, and the pace of recovery was expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels and lasting economic scars from the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU), mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no sign of large-scale fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activities and reduced credit demand amid recurring waves of the pandemic, total banking sector loans declined slightly in the second half of the year, but still registered a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant to the impact of the related downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again as COVID-19 infections resurged from the fourth quarter onwards. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development towards the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end, facilitating the normalisation and faster growth of the global economy. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets reached new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive easing may lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to scale back monetary accommodation earlier and ending financial markets’ expectations of a “low-for-longer” monetary policy. Over the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio inflows into the region rebounded and search-for-yield activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia continued to face persistent uncertainties arising from the pandemic. First, amid global competition for vaccines, the region’s less developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage or efficacy, together with weaker fiscal positions among governments in the region, could worsen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. In Mainland China, the economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to register positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will continue to depend heavily on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest market consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. After depreciating for several months in early 2020, the renminbi strengthened during the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened and the Mainland debt market recorded strong fund inflows. A detailed study shows that fundamentals, rather than market sentiment, played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations during the COVID-19 outbreak (see Box 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level. With a modest increase in domestic demand and further expansion in merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rebound in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. Nevertheless, real GDP fell by 6.1% for 2020 as a whole, the largest decline on record and, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019, the first-ever decline for two consecutive years. The latest sectoral GDP data show that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more sharply than the overall economy amid the pandemic. In response to the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist pandemic-affected sectors and members of the public and strengthen Hong Kong’s capacity to combat the pandemic. In the recent 2021/22 Budget, the Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy, including the distribution of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic Consumption Voucher Scheme and the provision of 100% guaranteed Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for the unemployed. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures were expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines offer hope that economic activities will return to normal, and the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. As widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, further strengthening of the Mainland economy is expected to support Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, its highest level since the SARS epidemic. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell markedly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and declined further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. Although the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. As global and domestic economic conditions remained challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong were likely to remain mild in the near term. In particular, slower growth in newly contracted private housing rentals would continue to restrain local inflation. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2021 was a moderate 1.4%, while the Government forecast the underlying and headline inflation rates for 2021 at 1.0% and 1.6% respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side CU against the US dollar, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including demand arising from buoyant initial public offering fundraising activities and southbound inflows through Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side CU was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side CU was triggered 85 times, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Analysed by geographical location, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no sign of large-scale fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the evolution of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong is able to withstand fund-flow volatility given its ample foreign reserves and robust banking system. As the triggering of the strong-side CU increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank interest rates generally remained extremely low. The composite interest rate, which reflects retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds, declined further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. As funding costs fell, the average lending rate for new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Alongside the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020. During most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium to the CNY exchange rate, with the premium averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with outstanding renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-boundary fund-flow channels connecting with the Mainland. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by gains in global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through southbound Stock Connect, the local equity market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose for several reasons, including unprecedented monetary easing by major economies; optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate the recovery of economic activities; and reduced global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses after a sharp decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and briefly surpassing the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and CNH debt markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded as market confidence recovered rapidly in response to unprecedented economic stimulus measures introduced by governments worldwide. Despite a modest rebound in bond yields during the same period, bond yields globally, including those in Hong Kong, remained close to historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expected the coronavirus pandemic to eventually end and global economic growth to accelerate thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a “low-for-longer” global monetary policy stance, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the buoyant expectations in financial markets were disconnected from the still challenging macroeconomic environment, and asset prices could become volatile if the economic recovery proved weaker than expected or policy support was withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, because inflation exceeded expectations). Looking ahead, policymakers will face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support and how to address the many legacies of the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and lasting economic scarring. Lingering uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continued to cloud the economic recovery in East Asia, while less developed emerging market economies in the region might face greater challenges in procuring and distributing vaccines. Any setback in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse the prevailing optimism and destabilise fund inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain and will depend largely on developments in the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The Government therefore announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of containing systemic risks. Benefiting from the release of purchasing power following economic reopening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, coronavirus infections have risen again, prompting governments to reimpose lockdowns and social distancing measures and causing global growth momentum to weaken once more. The emergence of more transmissible variants at the end of 2020 and their subsequent spread around the world made the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020 raised market expectations that the pandemic would eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normal and growth to accelerate. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery was continued policy stimulus, including major central banks’ commitment to a “low-for-longer” monetary policy stance amid subdued inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 forecast (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, the disconnect between strong financial market performance and the still challenging macroeconomic environment could expose asset markets to volatility amid multiple risks. First, the prospects for bringing the pandemic under control depend on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX facilitate more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supplies are expected to make the problem of low vaccination rates more severe in lower-income emerging market economies. If the pandemic is not brought under control as expected, social distancing measures and other restrictions may need to be extended, thereby undermining the prospects for global recovery. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population in selected economies having received at least one dose of vaccine (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets is predicated on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly a “low-for-longer” monetary policy stance. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen amid the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, while higher-than-expected inflation readings could also increase financial market volatility. Chart 2.4 US and euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, there is significant uncertainty surrounding future China-US relations. The trend towards China-US “decoupling”, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance towards Mainland China across both US political parties, this trend may not reverse under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. While premature withdrawal could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a “cliff effect”, these measures are costly over the longer term, including the fiscal burden they impose and their postponement of the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources, such as allowing “zombie firms” with no longer viable business models to survive on continued government support. In addition, policymakers must address the many legacies of the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 because of declining corporate income and surging government expenditure (Chart 2.5). Although the problems posed by the sharp rise in debt may not be imminent given the current exceptionally low level of global interest rates, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy concerns the long-term economic losses or lasting scarring that the pandemic may cause. For example, elevated uncertainty may prompt firms to reduce investment, while workers suffering from prolonged unemployment may permanently leave the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after plunging in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was driven mainly by a rebound in exports, with particularly strong export demand for electronic and technology equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers, continued to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite lingering uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment inflows have resumed. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted greater bond inflows owing to improved market sentiment and higher yields than bonds in advanced economies (Chart 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the launch of vaccine production programmes, equity inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly amid portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by about 10% from its low in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows East Asia continued to face lingering uncertainties surrounding the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offered hope to the region’s hard-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early vaccine batches increased procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also posed challenges to the region’s logistics and public health capabilities. As a result, less developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, while uneven vaccination across economies may prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related sectors. Second, as investor optimism was driven largely by the vaccine rollout, the prevailing rebound in fund inflows and financial asset prices could end if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination fell far short of expectations. A sudden decline in fund inflows could trigger another bout of market turbulence. With the coronavirus successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports also maintained growth, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-technology products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the coronavirus pandemic, Mainland GDP still grew by 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions of demand components to GDP growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the economic recovery will still depend in part on developments in the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have normalised, service sectors remained partially disrupted following renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. Externally, despite renewed export growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remained uncertain because of new waves of infections in most developed economies. In addition, China-US tensions may not ease in the near term. However, the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement and the agreed EU-China Comprehensive Agreement on Investment will help further integrate China with other economies and may partly offset the adverse impact of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Given that the economic outlook remains highly uncertain, the Government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not change significantly in 2021, in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of containing systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan prioritises technological self-reliance and dual circulation, with the aim of raising per capita GDP to the level of a moderately developed country by 2035. The coronavirus outbreak appears to have had only a limited impact on bond issuers’ repayment capability, with the overall default rate in the Mainland debt market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of bond defaults increased in 2020 because of a sharp rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises (Chart 2.9). Although the increase in defaults by state-owned enterprises mainly reflected the Central Government’s determination to break their “implicit guarantee” and promote more rational market risk pricing, limited fiscal space among some local governments, particularly those in less developed regions, may also have been a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Size and ratio of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, the cost of funding for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual interest rate normalisation contributed to some extent to the higher cost of funding for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields In the property market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities increased at a much slower pace (Chart 2.11). The housing oversupply problem that had troubled third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. At the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below its peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real gross domestic product remained far below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, with domestic demand picking up and merchandise exports expanding further. With COVID-19 vaccination raising hopes that economic activities will return to normal, the domestic economy is expected to resume growth in 2021 after recording its sharpest contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the domestic economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. The labour market is therefore expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures will remain mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activities remained far below their pre-pandemic level. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record. Following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, this also marked the first time in history that declines were recorded for two consecutive years. The latest sectoral GDP data also showed that economic activities in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Domestic private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, although consumer confidence remained weak as social distancing measures were reimposed amid the third and fourth local waves of the pandemic. Overall investment spending also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment improved temporarily. Partly benefiting from stronger exports, particularly to Mainland China, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism was still at a standstill. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged on GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower recovery in merchandise exports than in imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions from major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports In response to the prolonged pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totalling HK$30.4 billion between September and December 2020 to assist sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong’s capability to combat it. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the latest 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including issuing a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher under the Consumption Voucher Scheme and providing 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for unemployed persons. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced a further extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade finance facilities under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to facilitate the normalisation of economic activities, the Hong Kong economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the domestic economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, which will in turn affect Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021 as a whole, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed further to 7.2% in February 2021, the highest level in 17 years (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average salary index for employees, which reflects labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to help them retain employees. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the Government launched other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure because of weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the domestic labour market. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Domestic inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell markedly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Although the three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it also remained low. Specifically, price pressures on basic food eased, while the cost of meals bought away from home declined markedly, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway discounts while dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other tradable goods, such as durable goods, remained moderate. On the services front, the rental component of the composite consumer price index remained weak as private housing rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 Rental component of the composite consumer price index and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost As global and domestic economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should remain mild in the near term. In particular, domestic inflation will continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in the growth of newly signed private housing rentals. The market consensus forecast puts the headline inflation rate at a moderate 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 1% and the headline inflation rate at 1.6% for 2021. As inbound tourism rapidly plunged into a depression amid the COVID-19 pandemic, market concerns arose that the crisis could have scarring effects on the subsequent recovery of the labour market. Against this background, this Box provides an empirical analysis of the impact of an inbound tourism boom on Hong Kong’s labour market to shed light on the potential impact of the current tourism downturn. Inbound tourism has experienced dramatic ups and downs since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Visitor arrivals began to surge after the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply as individuals to visit Hong Kong once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding 7 days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry IVS endorsements permitting multiple visits to Hong Kong within one year. Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure links with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, while inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Taking the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We regard the introduction of the IVS in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock because its timing was nearly exogenous and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. The data used in our main analysis are drawn from population data in Hong Kong’s Population Censuses or By-censuses. Specifically, we use 5% samples from the Population Censuses or By-censuses of 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016. We also define tourism-related sectors as the catering, retail, hotel and transport sectors. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences analytical framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers aged 20-40 in the treatment group and older workers aged 41-65 in the comparison group. We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because, being at an early stage of their careers, they can respond to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism with greater flexibility in making major changes to their employment choices. As the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market may change over time, we also employ an event study to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers, particularly women and workers with only secondary education, were more likely to enter tourism-related sectors after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the impact of the IVS on the probability of younger women working in tourism-related sectors was especially significant and persistent, remaining close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards in terms of the average difference in the probability of entry relative to the older cohort (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare the income of workers in tourism-related sectors (the treatment group) with that of workers in non-tourism-related sectors (the comparison group). The estimates show that, following the implementation of the IVS, income growth among workers in tourism-related sectors was higher than among employees in non-tourism-related sectors. In addition, compared with similar employees in other sectors, female workers and workers with lower educational attainment in tourism-related sectors experienced larger and rising income gains of 3-20 percentage points (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the income of female and less-educated workers The above findings are broadly consistent with international experience, showing that tourism is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses showing that the strong growth in inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and enhanced the resilience of the labour market for the lower-skilled segment. As inbound tourism plunges from boom to trough, these groups of workers may be more severely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side CU, which was triggered multiple times during September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects. With the Aggregate Balance increasing to over HK$450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and lingering US-China tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is capable of withstanding pressures arising from fund-flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side CU, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects (Chart 4.1). Although some proceeds raised from initial public offerings were remitted out of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505–7.7544 in November and December amid improved sentiment in the local equity market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards year-end. With fundraising activities remaining buoyant in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. During the review period, the Aggregate Balance increased as the strong-side CU was triggered multiple times, reflecting substantial inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. During September and October 2020, the strong-side CU was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CU was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicated no sign of substantial outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual fund movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index broadly followed the US dollar’s weakening against major currencies and declined (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the REER broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and lingering US-China tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As an international financial centre where various fundraising activities, such as initial public offerings, take place, Hong Kong experiences substantial fund inflows and outflows. On the one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, Hong Kong is able to withstand fund-flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continued inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, local monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and recent months. In the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during the period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the repeated triggering of the strong-side CU. Meanwhile, the other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large initial public offerings led to increases in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise significantly from July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the completion of the initial public offerings and customers’ repayment of IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Moving into January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased sharply again, mainly driven by a large initial public offering at the end of January. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased by 21.7% during the seven-month period since the end of June, or by a modest 9.1% after excluding the effect of the initial public offering at the end of January. Analysed by counterpart assets and excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the Monetary Base resulting from the triggering of the strong-side CU (Chart 4.7). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period, or by a modest 9.1% after excluding the effect of the initial public offering at the end of January. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined amid low deposit rates, the decrease was more than offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Total foreign currency deposits increased steadily by 3.6% during the seven-month period since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from initial public offering activities, total deposits with authorized institutions increased sharply by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the initial public offering at the end of January, total deposits grew by a modest 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand as well as business- and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. As the Aggregate Balance increased, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large initial public offerings in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not fluctuate significantly owing to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Broadly tracking the US dollar yield curve, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level generally declined in line with Hong Kong dollar interbank rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects retail banks’ average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding, declined further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). With lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the one-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the US, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should remain low, with occasional fluctuations arising from capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide an adequate buffer to maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook for Mainland China than for the rest of the world, as well as US dollar weakness. FTSE Russell’s announcement at the end of September that Mainland government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index provided further investment demand supporting the strengthening of the renminbi. For most of the review period, the CNH traded at a premium to the CNY, averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained modest by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained stable during the review period. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations arising from occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, it remained below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). The three-month CNH HIBOR declined in late December in line with onshore renminbi interest rates, before rising again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Growth in renminbi deposits accelerated from the fourth quarter, reflecting to some extent renminbi appreciation and higher renminbi interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, increasing by 21.9% to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021 (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of the total, renminbi customer deposits increased by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, outstanding certificates of deposit declined by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion during the seven-month period since the end of June 2020. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, up by 16.7% from the same period a year earlier. Among these transactions, remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland grew faster than those from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong’s deep renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payment and financial transactions. For 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system (RTGS) reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Retail banks’ profit in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020 and their asset quality also deteriorated slightly, as the economic downturn persisted amid recurring waves of the coronavirus pandemic and the prolonged low interest rate environment. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient, underpinned by its continued strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures to continue supporting the broader economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and persistent geopolitical tensions will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the associated downside risk factors on its asset quality. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% in the second half of 2020 compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, from 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed to 1.01% in the second half of 2020 from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decline in net interest income that more than offset the slight increase in non-interest income and led to lower profit. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, while the return on assets declined to 0.77% from 1.19% in 2019. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant, largely due to substantial fund inflows driven by stock market activities. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (a measure of the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost for retail banks) broadly followed a similar trend, declining markedly to 0.28% at the end of 2020 from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong declined moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks’ net interest margins. In addition, despite breakthroughs in vaccine development that boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the banking sector’s loan quality and profitability in the near term. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of locally incorporated AIs The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated stable funding positions among AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5%, respectively, in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and stable funding positions of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all AIs, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 The liability structure of all AIs As total deposits of all AIs increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans declined during the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all AIs fell to 72.3% at the end of 2020 from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, the average Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio and foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0%, respectively, at the end of 2020, from 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a persistent economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tighter social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, total credit in the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although its growth rate slowed markedly to 1.2% from 6.7% in 2019. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all AIs declined by 1.8% in the second half of 2020 after growing by 3.0% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2%, respectively, in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans remained broadly unchanged at the end of 2020 compared with the end of June, after declining by 2.0% in the first half. Foreign currency loans decreased by 4.5% in the second half of 2020 after growing markedly by 10.6% in the first half, partly reflecting weaker demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector became slightly more optimistic about the near-term credit demand outlook than six months earlier. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020 showed that the share of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase in the following three months rose to 37%, while the share expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Banks’ loan quality deteriorated slightly as the pandemic adversely affected the repayment capability of households and corporates, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio of all AIs rose moderately to 0.9% at the end of 2020 from 0.79% six months earlier, while the overdue and rescheduled loans ratio of all AIs increased to 0.57% at the end of 2020 from 0.49% at the end of June 2020. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loans ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48%, respectively (Chart 5.13).

Moving into 2022, the global economy performed weakly, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify across economies, particularly in the US. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic and the possibility that monetary policy tightening may be more aggressive than expected if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. If the US Fed tightens monetary policy substantially and thereby tightens global financial conditions, the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies will come under pressure. More recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have a significant impact on the global economy through trade and financial channels and further complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, growth in total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the continued economic recovery, while US monetary policy normalisation may proceed faster than expected. These risk factors will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness extending into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on mobility worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and became broad-based across goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the US. More recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, surging commodity prices may further heighten the threat of global inflation, while increased financial market volatility may lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties. In the near term, large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic could lead to renewed lockdowns and a further deterioration in supply bottlenecks. In the US, as the risk of inflation proving more persistent and broad-based than expected increased, the US Fed turned more hawkish, accelerating the timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. If the US Fed needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions may also tighten, weakening borrowers’ debt-servicing ability, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. More recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may pose the risk of sustained increases in global commodity prices, aggravate shortages of industrial goods and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during market stress, as well as the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although renewed stringent COVID-19 restrictions in some Southeast Asian economies temporarily slowed the recovery momentum in the third quarter, while the region’s technology-product exporting economies, namely South Korea and Singapore, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and constrained public health resources. Second, faster policy normalisation by the US Fed may trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures. Economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery will face an increasingly difficult trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. Third, slower growth in major economies, together with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the outlook for trade growth. Fourth, increases in various commodity prices arising from the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to inflation in the region while weakening consumption. Together with increased global economic uncertainties, this will further complicate decisions by regional central banks on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. Over the longer term, to rebuild sustainable and robust growth models, investors need to attach greater importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is affected by companies’ environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term owing to the persistent property market downturn and the outbreak of the Omicron variant. The Mainland authorities have therefore made stabilising growth their top priority this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. Total onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both declined in the second half of 2021. Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of state-owned enterprise bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risks to the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks, particularly systemically important banks, have limited loan exposure to developers, low non-performing loan ratios and high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product grew modestly, as merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the continued global economic recovery, improved local labour market conditions and the Government’s launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year comparison, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Moving into 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures weighed on economic activity in Hong Kong. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts and extended application and repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also available for loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the continuing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also support the economy. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product growth of 2.0% to 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to the uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below the pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that pressures in the labour market had re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected fewer new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tightened COVID-19 restrictions will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on developments in the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year comparison, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months, partly owing to increases in the prices of meals out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to increase slightly in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-induced disruptions to logistics. However, weak rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast is for a headline inflation rate of 2.4% in 2022, while the Government forecasts a headline inflation rate of 2.1% and an underlying inflation rate of 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local equity market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021, its appreciation subsequently lost momentum, mainly owing to weak southbound net buying through Stock Connect and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen alongside the US Fed’s monetary policy normalisation. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) range most of the time and continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Given ample interbank liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to thrive. In particular, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow, with the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022. Although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system rose to RMB1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from Hong Kong’s efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets generally higher in the final quarter of 2021, taking the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, mounting market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices and escalating Russia-Ukraine tensions have led major global equity markets to consolidate since early January 2022.

The global economy slowed markedly in late 2021 amid the rapid worldwide spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron) and persistent production bottlenecks, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and became broad-based across goods and services in major advanced economies (AEs), particularly the US. Heightened inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the Fed’s monetary policy stance, increasing the risk that a premature tightening of global financial conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuations and adversely affect emerging markets, where recoveries generally continued to lag. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered global financial market volatility, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant in the region, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with the region’s major exporters of technology products continuing to outperform other economies. While the Omicron variant is unlikely to seriously derail the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainties associated with new variants will continue to cloud the region’s economic outlook. Moreover, the Fed’s policy normalisation may trigger regional asset price corrections, while slowing growth in major economies may weigh on the region’s merchandise export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, raises commodity prices and inflation risks and, on the other hand, dampens consumption and increases global economic uncertainties, further complicating regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021 amid a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power shortages and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from the cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the government has made stabilising growth its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policies will become more supportive. The global economic recovery slowed visibly in the final quarter of 2021, as the spread of the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with that of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply-chain problems, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the persistent drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major AEs, and slowing growth momentum in Mainland China, which offset the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF real gross domestic product growth projections Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose markedly in major AEs, particularly the US, where larger-scale policy stimulus had been implemented since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures became broad-based across goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up the prices of a wide range of commodities and may exacerbate already-elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core consumer price index inflation in selected economies (1) The latest data for the US, the UK and the Euro area are for January 2022, while those for the others are for December 2021. (2) “Advanced Asia” includes Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) “Emerging market economies in Asia” include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, with risks tilted to the downside, and will depend on how the pandemic and related supply-chain disruptions evolve, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment, and major central banks’ policy responses to inflation.
