Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far responded to the recent surge in Omicron cases with targeted measures focused on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less stringent measures should help reduce supply-chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, renewed lockdowns cannot be ruled out in the event of large-scale outbreaks, which could lead to a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index – suppliers’ delivery times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to improve gradually, providing some relief from goods inflation. However, several developments may cause the current high global inflation to persist for longer than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices, the lagged pass-through of higher production costs to final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier surge in global residential property prices will drive future rent increases, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Fed shifted towards a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as “transitory” and doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from US$15 billion to US$30 billion per month, with a view to ending its asset purchase programme by March 2022, while also beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests that the Fed may raise interest rates multiple times during 2022. By contrast, the European Central Bank may face a more difficult policy trade-off given the Euro area’s closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine. Against this backdrop, coupled with persistently high global debt levels and asset valuations following a prolonged period of accommodative policies, if persistent inflationary pressures require the Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt servicing ability may be at risk of deteriorating and financial market volatility may be triggered. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe intensified, risk aversion in financial markets increased and signs of US dollar shortages emerged, including wider cross-currency swap spreads. Amid a premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce these funds’ liquidity risks during market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as the region’s major exporters of technology products, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the unevenness of the regional recovery. In addition, inflationary pressures remained moderate in several emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index Markets generally expect a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, but the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread across the region since late 2021, its economic impact has remained milder than that of previous waves of infection. However, some regional economies where vaccination rates continue to lag and public health resources are more constrained will remain exposed to the threat of new variants. Second, the Fed’s policy normalisation may trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. For regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support the economic recovery, the trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. At the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in long-term US yields may spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, increasing the risk of corrections in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the region’s merchandise trade outlook faces uncertainties from slowing major economies and a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which may weaken the region’s export growth. Chart 2.6 US: Imports from emerging Asia and real gross domestic product Fourth, while regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, increases in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will pass through to regional inflation while dampening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainties, this will further complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted regional economies to the longer-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to give greater weight to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 studies whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms’ environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic dealt a severe blow to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Outflows from some open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode Apart from investors’ liquidity needs, another possible reason for the substantial outflows was that investors exercised a “first-mover advantage” by redeeming their fund holdings early, thereby avoiding redemption costs that could surge during market stress. To curb outflows arising from the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing — a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, no empirical research had established whether swing pricing could effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this box conducts an empirical study to determine whether swing pricing reduced outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode and thereby lowered their liquidity risks. It also seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming before other investors and thereby passing redemption costs on to them. It mainly exists in open-ended funds using traditional pricing rules, under which fund investors’ subscription and redemption costs, such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments, are reflected in open-ended fund prices only after transactions take place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not bear those transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, particularly when large redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks facing open-ended funds.

Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021 amid sustained growth in merchandise exports and private consumption, recording its first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity. The overall economy is expected to remain on a recovery path in 2022 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the recovery will be subject to uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up in the near term alongside rising import prices, weak local rentals and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP expanded further by 5.5% in the third quarter and grew by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth moderated from the first half. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, private consumption increased on the back of improved labour market conditions and the Government's implementation of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. However, aggregate investment declined in the final quarter after rebounding strongly for two consecutive quarters. Externally, Hong Kong's merchandise trade remained robust amid the continued global economic recovery, while trade in services stayed weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Chart 3.2). On a net basis, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volumes A new wave of local infections and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to end-October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from the expansion of the global economy. The Government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also render support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2.0%–3.5% in 2022, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in previous chapters. In particular, recent pandemic developments, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns, such as the Russia-Ukraine situation, have clouded the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, if quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China resumes earlier than expected, local economic growth could be boosted. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent trough in February 2021, although it remained below the pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures had resurfaced amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also pointed to fewer new vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and tightened COVID-19 restrictions will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Further ahead, labour market conditions will depend on local pandemic developments and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures broadly increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, amid a recovery in local demand and rising external prices (Chart 3.5), prices of meals out and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the composite consumer price index continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour cost remained weak, it edged up in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong's import prices Chart 3.6 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals Chart 3.7 Unit labour cost Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-induced logistics disruptions. However, weak rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast puts the headline inflation rate at 2.4% in 2022, while the Government forecasts the headline and underlying inflation rates at 2.1% and 2.0% respectively for 2022.

Amid risk-off sentiment in the local equity market and concerns over US monetary policy normalisation, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. With ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) remained low. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties related to US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is able to withstand shocks arising from volatilities in fund flows. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed mostly on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings (CUs) and continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had softened gradually against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local equity market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through Stock Connect and market expectations of a stronger US dollar as the US Fed’s monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish (Chart 4.2). Initial public offering activities continued to support the Hong Kong dollar during the review period (Chart 4.3). Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no sign of unusual cross-boundary fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Southbound net buying through Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Despite a stronger US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) remained stable owing to the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) generally tracked the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties related to US monetary policy, the development of the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds, the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions, may weaken the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Hong Kong also has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is able to withstand volatilities in fund flows without compromising financial stability. Hong Kong’s monetary conditions remained accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 1.4% in the eight months since end-June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional bill issuance to meet banks’ continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance correspondingly declined by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion before Discount Window activities (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, Government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) In the six months since end-July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) increased modestly by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. It should, however, be noted that monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering-related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities. It is therefore more appropriate to observe the longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Overall, Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. With ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBORs remained low despite market concerns over US monetary policy tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of higher funding demand towards year-end, HIBORs edged up in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages increased slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system will provide a sufficient cushion in the event of large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The CNH interbank market continued to function normally during the review period. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced mild fluctuations in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 The overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. In the six months since end-July 2021, the outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit (CDs) increased by 30.3% to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Of these, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in outstanding CDs. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and CDs in Hong Kong During the six-month period since July 2021, although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022 (Chart 4.10), up by 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period a year earlier. Hong Kong’s deep renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payments and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Flows of renminbi trade settlement payments Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Major global equity markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated from January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong equity market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by sharp declines in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong drove the Hang Seng Index to a nearly two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s CNH debt market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market had softened since mid-2021, partly reflecting weaker asset market sentiment and a new wave of the local pandemic. Major global equity markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, driving the MSCI World Index to an all-time high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). The global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings, supported by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, underpinned gains in major global equity markets, although the pandemic remained investors’ principal risk concern throughout the year. However, major global equity markets consolidated from early January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies in the face of sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices and escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. By contrast, the Hong Kong equity market continued to lag behind other major global equity markets at the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November and closed at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, renewed buying interest from value investors in the Hong Kong equity market drove the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points at the end of February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index declined by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index Equity market option-implied volatilities fluctuated sharply in late November 2021 following the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, before receding. Although the SKEW Index had retreated from its all-time high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors’ concerns about a correction in the sustained equity market rally since the outbreak of the pandemic and their willingness to pay more to hedge against downside risks in equity markets (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and the S&P 500 Index, and the SKEW Index Against a backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong equity market continued to register net inflows from international investors since the previous report (Chart 4.13). By contrast, southbound Stock Connect recorded substantial net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns about the impact of Mainland regulatory changes on technology stocks. However, southbound buying through Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording total inflows of HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, the cumulative net buying amount increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net equity market fund inflows into Hong Kong Chart 4.14 Net flows through Stock Connect Hong Kong’s primary market slowed in the second half of 2021 after raising a record amount of funds in the first half. There were 98 new listings in 2021, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), with total funds raised down 17.8% from the preceding year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global initial public offering market, behind only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Initial public offering market in Hong Kong The outlook for the local equity market remains uncertain. Monetary policy easing in the Mainland and more secondary listings of US-listed Chinese companies in Hong Kong’s primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong equity market. However, the equity market continues to face numerous headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding the development of the local pandemic, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Retail banks’ profit declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio increased slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by both historical and international standards. With sound capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, the HKMA extended various support measures to further help the economy weather the difficult period. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, while the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation will also present challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 16.1% in the second half of 2021 compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was mainly attributable to declines in net interest and non-interest income and an increase in operating expenses. As a result, the return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Reflecting the continued impact of the low interest rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks also remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following increased issuance of Exchange Fund Bills by the HKMA, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose slightly in the final quarter of 2021. However, as liquidity in the banking system remained very abundant, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR increased slightly by 9 basis points from six months ago to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months ago to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Since June 2019, the composite interest rate has been calculated based on the new local “interest rate risk in the banking book” framework. As such, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those of previous months. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong increased slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding costs have been calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. As such, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Although US monetary policy normalisation may signal an improvement in banks’ profitability, the near-term improvement may be partly offset by two factors. First, although the Federal Reserve indicated that it would raise interest rates several times in 2022, past experience suggests that movements in local interest rates may lag behind those in US interest rates, particularly when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains very abundant. Therefore, improvements in banks’ net interest margins may take more time to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also create uncertainty over the pace of economic recovery, thereby exerting pressure on banks’ asset quality and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.2% at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.5), well above the international minimum requirement of 8%. The Tier 1 capital ratio and Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2%, respectively. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs recorded a healthy level of 7.9% at the end of 2021, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3%. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated position. 2. From 1 January 2013, locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with the revised Basel III capital adequacy framework. As such, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 151.9% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.6), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 59.1%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The latest Net Stable Funding Ratio also reflected a stable funding position of AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.3% in the third quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted considerable efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate goals and contributing to global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021 last year, we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 as a standalone report for the first time this year. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong’s banking system to climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and putting our commitments as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation into practice. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA’s major functions. Readers will learn about our specific measures and initiatives in this report, with the following being some of the highlights: Banks are exposed to climate risk in their day-to-day operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks’ resilience to climate change. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and explored how technology could help banks assess the impact of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we also shared with the industry sound practices on the proper management of these products to help banks strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives to address climate risk and promote the development of sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework, which will enhance financial market transparency and improve the alignment of green finance policies. Internationally, we are actively participating in a range of international organisations to help formulate policies for addressing climate change and assess its implications for financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a very challenging year for the global debt market, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record robust growth of 42%, with total issuance rising to US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong Asia’s largest centre for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the Hainan Provincial People’s Government, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and international markets. The flourishing of Hong Kong’s green bond market is also attributable in part to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing nearly US$16 billion worth of green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two “firsts”. In May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural Government retail green bonds totalling HK$20 billion, which were then the world’s largest retail green bond issuance. We also assisted the Government in issuing its inaugural tokenised green bond in February 2023. It was the world’s first tokenised green bond issued by a government, and the issuance also marked a milestone in successfully combining our strengths in the debt market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, data and talent are indispensable to the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and can only be built through the efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to developing a local green classification framework as mentioned above, the Steering Group has also promoted skills training in the industry and enhanced Hong Kong’s data resources through its Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance. The Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas, including mandatory climate-related disclosures and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, particularly by setting a target of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050. At the same time, we enhanced our risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and long-term risk-adjusted returns. In addition, to fully capture the potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment by the Exchange Fund and identifying investment opportunities that support the climate transition and climate change mitigation, thereby enhancing the portfolio’s long-term returns. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio was 43% lower than its 2017 level. Indeed, the Exchange Fund’s exposure to carbon-intensive assets has consistently remained below that of the broader market. Going forward, we will continue progressing towards our net-zero target by further integrating environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, continuing to collaborate with stakeholders, and focusing on portfolio decarbonisation and transition. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: environment, people and social responsibility. On the environmental front, we strive to promote a green workplace and more environmentally friendly markets for the wider community. On the people front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive workplace. On the social responsibility front, we seek to enhance financial literacy, promote financial inclusion and actively give back to the community. Compared with the levels in 2015, when we began tracking our carbon footprint, our per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper consumption all recorded double-digit reductions in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the near term, our targets are to eliminate Scope 1 emissions entirely and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030, using 2015 as the baseline. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration among multiple parties. On this important global issue, we recognise that we must take action and lead by example, while working with like-minded peers and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s near-term plans and priorities for addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in pursuing this goal. We are confident that, with the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the wider community, we can successfully meet the climate challenges ahead. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong’s financial sector and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable organisation. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development of, and best practices in, green and sustainable finance. As the banking regulator, we will strive to strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage banks to understand their progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate considerations into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework for the banking sector’s “greenness baseline”. Meanwhile, the HKMA will support banks’ efforts to enhance their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as by exploring different measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, quantify and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress tests as part of the regular regulator-led stress tests for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to withstand climate risks under an enhanced stress test framework covering various stress scenarios, including extreme climate conditions and adverse economic environments. To promote the sound development of banks’ provision of green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct an off-site Box assessment to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to further develop the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial sector’s green transition, the HKMA plans to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in increasing the issuance of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening the Programme’s scope to cover sustainability bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme to expand Hong Kong’s green finance talent pool. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. We will also continue to collaborate with other authorities and departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral issues such as skills training and data, green taxonomies, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will jointly launch various specialised initiatives in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market insights and targeted professional training for banks, and offering practical guidance to help banks formulate roadmaps for developing green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand its influence in Asia. The Alliance will also further strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate green finance knowledge sharing, and lead initiatives in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s investment portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to contributing to global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management processes, work towards its net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate action. As a responsible and sustainable organisation, the HKMA cares about its staff, the wider community and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continue to prioritise reducing carbon emissions and encourage staff to fully support energy conservation and waste reduction. In addition, we will provide staff with further guidance on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To advance digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications, further improving work efficiency while minimising, as far as possible, potential risks arising during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been working to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial system for a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to the impacts of various sustainability- and climate-related matters in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their important functions in the financial system and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has placed particular emphasis on building banks’ capabilities to respond to and manage climate risk, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crime and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 issued principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions to clarify how these risks are captured in the existing Basel Framework. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in 2021, the HKMA also maintained communication with banks to exchange views on the expectations, progress and challenges regarding implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into its banking supervisory processes and communicated it to the banking industry in June. As part of implementing the two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 “Risk-based Supervisory Approach” and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, drawing on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress test scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress tests into regular regulator-led stress tests, enabling a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. Meanwhile, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks associated with climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. In view of the increasing prevalence of green and sustainable products issued by banks, the HKMA conducted a round of thematic reviews focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified a number of sound practices during the thematic reviews and shared them with the industry in a circular issued in December, enabling banks to progressively strengthen their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks’ capabilities to manage climate risk. The HKMA has commenced the development of a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the BIS Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions could facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices; this work employs advanced analytics and regulatory technology, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the collection of anti-money laundering supervisory data to reduce banks’ manpower burden and paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and improve the consistency of green finance policies, the HKMA is collaborating with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. Commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, the framework classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to examine the framework’s features and challenges in depth, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the framework’s structure and core elements in the first half of 2023. Recognising that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its analysis and research on financial vulnerabilities to strengthen its ongoing surveillance. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its continuous monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On research, the HKMA conducted several applied research projects in 2022 to examine two major topics in depth, namely greenwashing3 in the corporate green bond market and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of these studies help inform the formulation of policy and supervisory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Locally, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared the research findings with a broad range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central banking research conferences and its Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s “Liquidity Facilities Framework” is a collateralised standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is exploring the incorporation of sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps promote international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, while drawing insights from these discussions to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA stepped up its efforts to raise market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), co-ordinates the financial sector’s response to climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategies1. The Steering Group’s work is primarily guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out 6 key long-term focus areas and 5 near-term action points to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem for a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Enhance climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre Promote the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection Enhance the relevant skills of practitioners and raise public awareness and understanding Encourage product innovation and initiatives to channel capital towards green and sustainable projects Capitalise on the opportunities presented by the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area) Strengthen regional and international collaboration Actions to date to advance sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Its current priorities include capacity building and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), green taxonomy (see “Developing a green classification framework to facilitate green finance” in the chapter “Building a sustainable financial system” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, in March, the Steering Group published a preliminary feasibility assessment of carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong and will support Hong Kong’s development into a regional carbon trading centre, including developing a high-quality international voluntary carbon market and capitalising on opportunities arising from collaboration within the Greater Bay Area. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability and sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of the collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire for non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which facilitates corporate sustainability reporting while helping financial institutions collect and analyse company-level data for risk assessment and relevant business decisions. This represents an important step in expanding the coverage of the Steering Group’s data work to include SMEs, a previously difficult-to-reach yet important segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to co-ordinate the efforts of financial regulators, government agencies, industry stakeholders and academia in capacity building and policy development, and to establish resources and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched 3 repositories respectively covering data, training information and internship opportunities to help the financial sector and other sectors access green and sustainable finance-related data and learning resources. Repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong To support industry capacity building, the Centre helped the Government launch the “Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme” in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and skills enhancement. Other capacity-building initiatives included launching the “Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative” to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new “Green and Sustainable Finance” module3 under the HKMA’s “Enhanced Competency Framework” for banking practitioners. “Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme” The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Alliance for Green Commercial Banks”4, bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutions and innovation and technology providers in the region to develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential to make green finance a mainstream core business and facilitate the financial system’s participation in global climate change-related activities. How it works Provide financial institutions with a one-stop peer-learning platform to access the knowledge, tools and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform themselves into credible green financial institutions Bring together green finance leaders, connect green financial institutions across different emerging markets, facilitate dialogue and explore frontier issues Advance the global green finance agenda and unlock vast green and climate-related investment opportunities In June, 5 leading global financial institutions5 became cornerstone members of the Alliance and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to facilitate the transition to a green economy. In addition, 3 global partners and 1 knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone members, International Finance Corporation and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtables, attracting over 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022, the Alliance and the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7 jointly published their first frontier research report, entitled “Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulatory Oversight”. The HKMA has continued to promote green and sustainable debt issuance and foster a local ecosystem of related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022, including bonds and loans, reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion) To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promote green finance, and develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in implementing the related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued close to US$16 billion equivalent of institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance the Programme’s transparency and accountability, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. To enable the public to participate in and share the benefits of Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment, the inaugural retail green bonds totalling HK$20 billion were issued in May and received an enthusiastic public response, making them the world’s largest retail green bond issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable finance products in Hong Kong and strengthened Hong Kong’s position as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular institutional green bond issuances in the 2022-23 financial year and issued US$5.75 billion equivalent of green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency offering covered US dollar, euro and renminbi tranches with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The offering was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in the Government’s previous green bond issuances, reflecting investors’ confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The shares allocated to international investors and Mainland investors participating through the southbound Bond Connect also increased, showcasing Hong Kong’s role as a premier offshore renminbi business hub and further consolidating its leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing an institutional tokenised green bond to test the use of distributed ledger technology in bond issuance and settlement. It was the first tokenised green bond issued by a government globally. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis over a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes, including coupon payment, settlement of secondary market trading and redemption at maturity, also digitalised. The experience gained from this Government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in undertaking similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and readily accessible market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association’s report showed that in 2022 Hong Kong became the largest arranging hub for international green and sustainable bond issuances in Asia, with bonds arranged in Hong Kong totalling US$27.8 billion and accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. Largest arranging hub for international green and sustainable bond issuances in Asia US$27.8 billion Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government again issued RMB5 billion of offshore local Government Bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the People’s Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. These issuances once again highlighted Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its longstanding position as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” launched in 2021 and leveraged the Scheme to attract more related professional service providers, including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external reviewers, to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been well received by the industry. As at the end of 2022, the Scheme had covered the costs of pre-issuance, post-issuance or both types of external review services for issuers of more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the Scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan size threshold for external review cost subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof of concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre collaborated again under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards, also known as mitigation outcome interests (MOIs), with a view to enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental attributes of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022 and successfully developed two prototypes that used blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment. As early as 2015, it took the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets, required its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrated environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Investing prudently according to the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term growth thereafter”, the HKMA believes that due regard to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate the associated risks. In the face of growing climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance its responsible investment journey, including setting a “Net-zero Emissions by 2050” target in 2022 and enhancing its risk management strategy to strengthen portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively contributes to building the green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment and collaborating with international organisations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risk. To fulfil its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI－Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS－Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD－Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the Exchange Fund’s investments. The primary guiding principle is that the HKMA gives priority to ESG investments if their risk-adjusted long-term returns are comparable to those of other investments, in line with the Exchange Fund’s investment objectives. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, oversees ESG and climate-related risks associated with the Exchange Fund’s investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors progress in ESG integration and the Exchange Fund’s ESG profile through regular reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for co-ordinating and overseeing the various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The proposals discussed and progress made at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Oversight and governance structure for responsible investment A dedicated team in the Risk Management and Compliance Division works closely with the investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investments: Public market investments The Credit, Rules and Compliance Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Compliance Division participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Striving for active ownership” under the “Risk Management” section on page 27 for details). Private market investments The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal conducted by the Risk Management and Compliance Division and the private market investment teams. Concrete evidence² continues to point to the significant impact of climate change and related risks. According to the latest report3 of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming that the announced “Nationally Determined Contributions” targets of all regions are fully implemented, the increase in global temperature by 2100 is still estimated to reach as high as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting the increase in global average temperature to below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and asset repricing by the market in anticipation of future trends, together with inherent physical risks, will intensify pressure on asset valuations. In view of updates to the global warming trajectory and model assumptions, the HKMA drew on the expertise of external consultants to further assess the resilience of the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” under a “Rapid Transition” scenario (Figure 2), in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021. The “Rapid Transition” scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments combine to drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are abruptly divested to keep the increase in average temperature within 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2100. The scenario is broadly aligned with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The “Investment Portfolio” remains resilient over the medium to long term because a relatively large proportion of its asset allocation consists of sovereign bonds that are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sectoral distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets may benefit from the transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may adversely affect performance in the short term, particularly that of equity assets. The “Investment Portfolio” as a whole will suffer increasingly severe impacts from physical risks that gradually materialise over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Like other modelling approaches, climate scenario analysis has its limitations. The analysis is based on sector weightings in market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level and does not take into account the effects of actively selecting specific securities within a sector. More in-depth analysis indicates that investments in the “Investment Portfolio” are generally more resilient to, or less affected by, transition shocks than the strategic asset allocation market benchmarks. This result reaffirms that the HKMA’s responsible investment approach focused on combating climate change can enhance portfolio resilience. The climate change trajectory remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund’s resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities arising from climate change. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and capturing opportunities relating to climate transition, climate risk mitigation and enhancement of long-term portfolio returns. Building on its strong momentum, the HKMA increased its holdings of green, social and sustainability bonds by a further 50% in 2022. In equity investments, the HKMA invests in an actively managed governance-themed equity portfolio and adopts a decarbonisation strategy for passive equity portfolios that tilts towards companies with lower carbon emissions. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with the general partners of the Exchange Fund’s “Long-Term Growth Portfolio” the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Figure 3). Figure 3 Ongoing measures to increase ESG investments The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator that, in addition to producing clean energy, places great emphasis on social and natural biodiversity factors. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain species of vultures. Livestock are important assets for the local villagers. To help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the animals from natural predators. The operator also employs bird-monitoring teams to issue alerts when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left by predators, allowing the wind turbines to be shut down to prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation creates a win-win outcome: it protects the villagers’ livelihoods while reducing fatal collisions between vultures and wind turbines, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can create more business opportunities and open up revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operation. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China specialising in logistics services for cold-chain pharmaceuticals, chemicals and high-end consumer goods. The company faces increasingly stringent ESG operating standards, mainly because its multinational corporate clients require service providers to meet ambitious decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these requirements, the company engaged an external consultant to help formulate a “Three-year ESG Plan” to reduce its carbon emissions intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan delivered significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures earned the company a “Low-carbon Green Management Case” award from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing. These achievements and recognition have enabled the company to secure substantial business opportunities, particularly from multinational clients in the consumer and chemical products sectors that place a strong emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its 4th annual ESG Workshop, exchanging sound ESG practices with 9 participating private market institutions, including general partners, limited partners and corporates, and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In public markets, the HKMA urges its trading counterparties, mainly investment banks, to expand their ESG staffing and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. Mr Howard Lee, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivers the opening remarks at the HKMA ESG Workshop 2022 At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in developing industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in a PRI-co-ordinated collaborative initiative among signatories to develop standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaires5, 6 for private equity and venture capital investments, helping private market investors conduct ESG assessments of general partners and investment proposals.
