In terms of social responsibility, the HKMA encourages staff to participate in volunteer and charitable activities; considers engaging social enterprises in procurement; promotes consumer education on financial services; and works with the banking industry to ensure equitable access to basic banking services for all sectors of society. The remainder of this chapter sets out details of the above strategies. Under the HKMA’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Risk Committee2, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the potential risks and threats facing the HKMA in its daily operations, including those arising from climate change. The physical impacts of climate change, such as flooding or other damage caused by more extreme weather events, may affect the HKMA’s offices and impede staff travel. To manage physical risks, the HKMA regularly updates its business continuity plans to address extreme weather conditions. The HKMA also conducts regular evacuation and backup facility activation drills to ensure that staff are always prepared to implement business continuity measures. A range of measures to mitigate potential risks has also been incorporated into office design. Transition risks may affect the HKMA’s energy use, air travel and waste disposal. The HKMA has been monitoring its exposure to transition risks by tracking its greenhouse gas emissions, waste generation, energy consumption and paper consumption. The HKMA’s climate target is to achieve net-zero Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 (air travel) greenhouse gas emissions across all areas of its corporate operations by 2050 or earlier. As a near-term emissions reduction target, the HKMA plans to eliminate Scope 1 emissions completely by converting all its existing vehicles to electric vehicles; and, using 2015 as the base year, to reduce Scope 2 emissions intensity by 63% by 2030 or earlier through various decarbonisation and offsetting strategies. Despite the challenges in determining Scope 3 emissions, the HKMA will adopt a multi-pronged approach, as far as practicable, to minimise Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions, such as those arising from paper consumption, waste generation and air travel. The HKMA’s long-term and near-term emissions reduction targets were developed with reference to the Science Based Targets initiative methodology, which was also validated by the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency. The HKMA has appointed the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency to verify the emissions, energy and paper consumption, and waste data6 disclosed in this report. The scope and basis of verification are set out in the “Verification Statement” section of this report. In 2023, in addition to publishing the Annual Report 2022, the HKMA issued its first standalone Sustainability Report 2022. The HKMA’s efforts to enhance ESG reporting were recognised with an ESG Award in the Public Sector/Not-for-profit Organisations category of the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants’ Best Corporate Governance and ESG Awards 2023. The HKMA was the first financial regulator to receive an award in this category. The judging panel commended the HKMA for achieving good ESG standards, producing a clear and readable Sustainability Report, and demonstrating its commitment to highly transparent and accountable reporting by appointing an independent body to verify its target-setting methodology and the environmental data disclosed in the report. In addition, the HKMA received the highest accolade, the Gold Award in the Non-profit Making and Charitable Organisations category, at the Hong Kong Management Association’s Best Annual Reports Awards 2023. The judging panel commended the HKMA’s annual report for clearly presenting comprehensive financial information and making effective use of infographics, demonstrating the HKMA’s determination to enhance financial literacy and promote financial inclusion. In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, its staff and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has awarded the HKMA the “15 Years Plus Caring Organisation” logo for 17 consecutive years since 2006. The HKMA is committed to properly managing the environmental impact of its operations, and its internal Green Office Guidelines provide guidance to staff on resource use and office waste generation. The HKMA has incorporated environmental considerations into the design, operation and maintenance of its owned and leased offices. When refurbishing offices, existing furniture and fitting-out materials are reused wherever possible to reduce waste, while environmentally friendly construction and decorative materials are given priority. The HKMA has consistently followed this approach, and the refurbished areas of its offices at Two International Finance Centre were awarded Gold certification under LEED7 and BEAM Plus Interiors8 in 2021 and 2022 respectively. Enhancing energy efficiency by adopting new technologies and making better use of existing ones remains one of the HKMA’s priorities. In addition to promoting good practices, such as switching off unnecessary lighting in work areas outside office hours to save electricity, other energy-saving measures include using light-emitting diode lighting, motion sensors, setting air-conditioned room temperatures at appropriate levels, and optimising energy use in the information technology network infrastructure. The HKMA’s energy consumption continued to decline, reaching 2.59 MWh9 per person in 2023, down 29.7% from the 2015 baseline (Figure 1). Given the nature of the HKMA’s daily operations, its greenhouse gas emissions mainly arise from the consumption of electricity generated from fossil fuels. In 2023, the combined intensity of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from purchased fuel and electricity was 1.48 tCO e10 per person, down 45.2% from 2015 (Figure 2). In addition to standardising equipment, office software and meeting facilities, the HKMA has adopted digital tools and technologies, and automated and streamlined workflows to create a digital workplace and enhance online collaboration within the organisation.11 Paperless meetings have become the HKMA’s primary mode of meeting. To further reduce paper consumption and improve efficiency, internal administrative matters are mainly handled through electronic processes. In addition, the HKMA encourages staff to embrace green and digital ways of working by replacing paper documents and communications with digital alternatives. Work is also under way to implement an electronic recordkeeping system. The above green and digital initiatives have produced positive results. In 2023, the HKMA’s paper consumption intensity was 11.55 kg per person, a substantial decrease of 64.8% from 2015 (Figure 3). As most international events resumed in-person formats after the COVID-19 pandemic, and given the need to promote the development of Hong Kong as an international financial centre, overseas business travel by relevant HKMA staff was unavoidable. To reduce carbon emissions from air travel, the HKMA encourages staff attending overseas events to take direct flights or combine different business trips where practicable. At the organisational level, the HKMA reduced its Scope 3 emissions by 126 tCO e in 2023 through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel. In addition, the HKMA participated in a Gold Standard12-certified carbon offset programme to offset the remaining carbon emissions from air travel; the programme covers waste-to-energy, solar power generation, and the provision of efficient and cleaner cooking facilities in developing countries. The HKMA will continue to make similar arrangements in 2024. The HKMA’s procurement process takes sustainability and environmental considerations into account. As part of a comprehensive review of the organisation’s procurement policies and procedures, the existing practice of procuring green products has been formalised, in compliance with the environmental specifications in the Government’s Green Procurement List, particularly for the procurement of electrical appliances and office consumables. ESG factors and innovative proposals that help enhance productivity and efficiency have also been incorporated into tender evaluation criteria. At the same time, all suppliers are required to undertake to comply with environmental regulations. In accordance with the “4R” principles, namely Refuse, Reduce, Reuse and Recycle, the HKMA adopts a three-pronged approach to minimising waste generation and managing waste disposal. In addition, the HKMA conducted two waste audits in 2022 and 2023 to facilitate the development of targeted waste management strategies. A breakdown of non-hazardous waste generated, including general waste sent to landfill and various types of recyclable waste, is provided in the “Performance Summary” section on page 56. In 2023, the HKMA participated directly for the first time in the red packet recycling programme organised by the management company of the International Finance Centre office building. Staff handed in about 3,000 used red packets that remained in pristine condition. These red packets were subsequently passed to an environmental organisation for distribution to the public for use during the following Lunar New Year. As the HKMA’s operational and backup data centres account for a major share of its overall energy consumption, both data centres have been upgraded to meet the highest standards set by BEAM Plus for existing data centres and achieve optimal Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE)13. In 2023, the HKMA’s two data centres were awarded “Gold” and “Platinum” ratings respectively under the BEAM Plus Existing Data Centres assessment guidelines issued in 2021; the HKMA is the first and only organisation in Hong Kong to have received these ratings. Enhancing the energy efficiency of the two data centres has long been a priority for the technical team. To this end, the team adopted green designs in renovation works and implemented energy-efficient good practices to lower PUE and achieve the relevant targets, including round-the-clock monitoring of the data centres’ environmental facilities and continuous improvement of environmental factors such as airflow and temperature settings. As the technical team continued to improve energy use in the data centres, the HKMA engaged an external consultant in December 2021 to conduct a review to comprehensively assess the data centres’ green performance and formulate recommendations for further improvements across various areas. The study was completed in mid-2022. Shortly after its completion, the HKMA also began preparations to obtain Green Data Centre certification under the BEAM Plus certification scheme. The certification process was highly comprehensive and rigorous. Throughout 2023, the technical team implemented enhancement measures based on the recommendations in the consultant’s report, covering areas ranging from energy performance to health-related aspects of the working environment within the data centres.

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency conducted an independent verification of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s (“HKMA”) 2023 environmental data (“2023 Data”). The 2023 Data comprise total energy consumption, Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions, greenhouse gas emissions from business air travel, paper consumption, and non-hazardous waste generated (including general waste sent to landfills and recyclable waste) in 2023, together with their respective intensities and changes compared with 2015 levels. In addition, the 2023 Data include the amount of food waste generated during the year, its intensity and the change compared with the level when the HKMA launched its food waste recycling programme in November 2022. The HKMA’s greenhouse gas emissions data were prepared in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (“GHG Protocol”) jointly published by the World Resources Institute and the World Business Council of Sustainable Development. The scope of verification covered the relevant data for the period from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2023, as well as the relevant data for the period from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2015 used for annual performance comparison (except for food waste). The scope of verification covered a total of 5 office and warehouse premises, comprising 4 offices located at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) One Pacific Place, and 4) Kowloon Commerce Centre, and a warehouse at 5) Roxy Industrial Centre in Kwai Chung. The objective of the verification was to provide reasonable assurance as to the accuracy and reliability of the 2023 Data and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA’s data collection mechanism. Within the scope of verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency reviewed selected representative data and supporting evidence from the 5 premises. The verification was performed in accordance with International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information”, issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were designed to form an opinion and conclusion to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification process was conducted in accordance with the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification process tested the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing selected sample data to their sources, and also reviewed the underlying procedures for data collection, aggregation, estimation, calculation and internal checking and performed reliability tests. The verification process also included verifying the internal data collection and management mechanism, interviewing representatives responsible for preparing the 2023 Data, and selecting representative data and information for examination. The relevant source data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the information. Our verification work was wholly independent and impartial. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency verification team was not involved in the preparation of the 2023 Data. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance on the 2023 Data and concludes that: the 2023 Data are materially accurate and reliable; and the HKMA’s overall data collection mechanism is adequate. Shum Siu Yan Audit Director Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency April 2024

The threat posed by climate change is imminent, making it imperative to accelerate global climate action. The World Meteorological Organization confirmed 2024 as the warmest year on record and the first year in which global temperatures exceeded the critical threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Meanwhile, although global greenhouse gas emissions eased slightly during the COVID-19 pandemic, they have recently reached a new high, underscoring the inadequacy of current climate change mitigation measures. As efforts to address global warming continue, climate-related risks are bound to intensify, with unpredictable implications for the economy and financial markets. Moreover, current geopolitical tensions, the growing fragmentation of the global economic landscape, the risk of worsening energy security issues, and uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook are all making it more challenging for countries to address climate change. The transition to a low-carbon economy requires substantial and sustained financial support. Globally, Asia faces particularly acute transition challenges. As the World Economic Forum has noted, Asia is not only an engine of global economic growth but also the region most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Asia therefore plays a pivotal role in determining whether the world can successfully achieve net-zero emissions. As Asia’s leading international financial centre, Hong Kong must strengthen its leadership role and fully harness the power of finance to support and drive the region’s transition. To this end, the HKMA announced the “Sustainable Finance Action Agenda” last year, setting out our vision and roadmap for progressively embedding sustainability into the core of the financial system. Our work focuses both on strengthening the financial sector’s capacity to address climate change-related risks and on helping the sector capture the emerging opportunities. At the same time, we lead by example. The HKMA’s sustainability work spans four key areas: supporting the banking sector in achieving net zero, investing in a sustainable future, financing net zero, and making sustainability more inclusive. The banking system plays a pivotal role in Hong Kong’s and Asia’s net-zero transition, but banks themselves also face considerable risks in the process. Under the “Action Agenda”, we have set ambitious targets requiring all banks to strive to achieve net-zero emissions in their own operations by 2030 or earlier and net-zero financed emissions by 2050 or earlier. We also require all banks to enhance their disclosures of climate change-related risks and opportunities. While continuing to strengthen banks’ climate risk management, we also provide guidance on transition planning to help them enhance their transition capabilities and better manage the associated risks. We are also undertaking preparatory work with relevant stakeholders to align Hong Kong’s sustainability disclosure requirements with international standards, with a view to further enhancing transparency in the industry’s related activities. In addition, we are refining the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance launched in May last year to include more sustainable activities, including transition activities. By providing clear criteria, we aim to channel more capital into sustainability- and transition-related projects. Climate change poses significant physical and transition risks that may affect the long-term financial performance and value of the Exchange Fund’s investments. At the same time, it also presents opportunities for the Exchange Fund to achieve growth and drive positive impact. Our experience has demonstrated that investment returns and positive sustainability impacts can be aligned and are not mutually exclusive. In view of this, we are committed to achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” by 2050 or earlier and, under the “Action Agenda”, have pledged to support Asia’s climate transition through the Exchange Fund’s investments. Sustainable investments currently account for more than 10% of the “Investment Portfolio”. To further promote sustainable investment in the region, the HKMA established strategic partnerships with the Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the International Finance Corporation in November last year to accelerate Asia’s transition to a low-carbon economy through co-investments. We also published the inaugural “HKMA ESG Expectations” document in September last year to further encourage fund managers to practise active ownership and adopt sound sustainable investment practices. Financing is particularly important for accelerating the region’s transition. As an international financial hub and the preferred venue for arranging international sustainable bond issuances by Asian issuers, including Mainland provincial and municipal governments, Hong Kong plays an important role in channelling capital to accelerate the region’s transition. The “Action Agenda” outlines a vision to develop Hong Kong into the region’s preferred sustainable financing platform and a goal of fostering sustainable finance innovation. From leveraging the demonstrative effect of the “Government Sustainable Bond Programme” to promote green bond innovation, including the issuance of the world’s first multi-currency digital bonds in February last year, to expanding the scope of subsidies under the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” to cover transition finance instruments in May last year, and launching the “Digital Bond Grant Scheme” in November last year, we have consistently sought to encourage regional issuers to use Hong Kong’s financial platform to raise the capital required for the decarbonisation transition. A robust transition requires not only capital and innovation, but also the support of an inclusive and accessible sustainability ecosystem. This includes reliable sustainability data, highly transparent disclosures, and industry professionals equipped with relevant knowledge and skills. In this regard, under the “Action Agenda”, we have pledged to support high-quality and comprehensive sustainability disclosures and to help bridge the region’s sustainable finance talent and knowledge gaps. We have made good progress in supporting relevant stakeholders and facilitating sustainability disclosures, particularly by providing convenient and user-friendly climate disclosure templates to promote sustainability disclosures by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). In November last year, we also launched the “Green and Sustainable Finance” Professional Level module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners to strengthen the relevant knowledge and skills of local banking practitioners. In addition, through the inaugural Hong Kong Green Week held in February last year and other events, we engaged people from different sectors in sustainability discussions, thereby fostering collaboration and innovation. Within the HKMA, we are committed to ensuring that our operations align with our sustainability vision. Under the “Action Agenda”, we have pledged to achieve net-zero emissions in our own operations by 2030 or earlier, 20 years ahead of our original commitment. We are also actively preparing to meet international sustainability disclosure standards in accordance with the roadmap issued by the Government. We began using electric vehicles in 2024 and incorporated low carbon emissions as a selection criterion in our procurement process. At the same time, we continue to enhance operational efficiency through digitalisation, foster a culture of sustainability within the organisation, and inspire staff to participate actively in sustainability efforts. Multilateral cooperation has always been a cornerstone of the global response to climate change, but the reshaping of the international landscape and dramatic geopolitical shifts have introduced greater uncertainty into global climate action. Yet climate change is an indisputable fact and is progressively intensifying. The current circumstances leave no room for complacency in addressing climate change. We firmly believe that advancing an orderly and inclusive transition will help mitigate the impact of climate risk on Hong Kong’s financial system while creating opportunities for us in the process. As we enter 2025, we will continue to forge ahead, do our utmost to advance sustainability, and deepen our relationships with like-minded partners. Despite the formidable challenges, we will remain steadfast in supporting the building of a sustainable future for Hong Kong, Asia and beyond.

Climate change is a major challenge facing the present generation. As an international financial centre and a sustainable finance hub in Asia, Hong Kong is committed to playing a pioneering role in supporting sustainable development in Asia and globally. In October 2024, the HKMA published the “Sustainable Finance Action Agenda” (the “Action Agenda”), setting out the HKMA’s vision in this area, including our future direction, the timelines for achieving the various targets, and how we expect the industry to work together to advance the relevant initiatives. Through strategic policy development, enhanced supervisory engagement and improvements to internal operations, the HKMA plans to strengthen the capacity of Hong Kong’s financial sector and the HKMA itself to address climate change risks, and to promote Asia’s transition towards a more sustainable economy. Through active participation in international and regional discussions, the HKMA also seeks to exert influence and contribute to the formulation of green and sustainable finance policies and standards at the regional and global levels. As the banking regulator, the HKMA focuses on enhancing the banking sector’s climate resilience and supporting banks in maintaining safety and soundness during the transition to net zero emissions. Our key priorities for 2025 include: - commencing a new round of thematic examinations of banks’ climate risk management practices and conducting a third round of consultations to assess banks’ implementation of the HKMA’s relevant supervisory requirements and further strengthen their climate risk management capabilities; - completing the incorporation of climate risk stress tests into the HKMA’s supervisor-led stress testing framework; - continuing to advance the incorporation of climate considerations into the HKMA’s supervisory review process; - commencing preparatory work to formulate relevant supervisory requirements for implementing in the local banking sector the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s forthcoming Pillar 3 disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks and the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards (ISSB Standards); - completing the preparation of a new Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-2 to provide banks with guidance on transition planning; and - sharing with the industry good practices in climate risk management and the application of green fintech. In addition to its role as the banking regulator, the HKMA also acts as a facilitator, promoting the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem and supporting banks in financing the transition. We published Phase 1 of the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance, providing the industry with a tool to identify green and sustainable economic activities and facilitate the associated flow of funds. The HKMA has commenced work on Phase 2 of the taxonomy to broaden its coverage, including the addition of transition elements and more green economic activities, as well as the incorporation of climate change adaptation objectives. Furthermore, building on the success of the third FiNETech event in 2024 and the Green Fintech Competition in 2023, we will organise another green fintech event in 2025 to promote banks’ adoption of green fintech solutions. Hong Kong is well positioned to support sustainable financing needs in the region. To reinforce this role, we will continue to assist the Government in implementing the Government Sustainable Bond Programme, whose expanded scope will cover sustainable projects such as social responsibility projects. This will help deepen the development of the local green and sustainable bond market and set an example for other potential issuers in the region. In addition, we will continue to provide subsidies through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme to encourage more borrowers in the region to raise sustainable funds using Hong Kong’s financing platform. We will also step up promotional efforts to encourage more governments, institutions and corporates from the Mainland and other regions to raise green funds in Hong Kong. At the same time, we will continue to catalyse and support sustainable finance innovation, including by providing subsidies to prospective issuers of digital green bonds through the Digital Bond Grant Scheme. Despite growing market demand for high-quality sustainability disclosures by institutions and corporates, different entities vary in their capacity and readiness to make such disclosures, and some may require additional guidance and support. In view of this, the HKMA will continue to work with other members of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group to make sustainability disclosures more accessible and inclusive. For example, we will continue to provide banks and their customers with a wider range of climate disclosure tools, including user-friendly sustainability disclosure templates and supporting tools; explore how technology can be used to make existing resources more readily accessible; and collaborate with major local industry bodies to provide the training needed by the industry. The sustainable finance market is evolving rapidly, requiring an expansion of the local talent pool and the closing of knowledge gaps in Hong Kong and across the region. The HKMA’s key priorities for 2025 include collaborating with the banking industry to develop professional-level training programmes for the “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners, and identifying areas in which the industry has further training needs through the forthcoming “Capacity Building for Future Banking 2026–2030” study. In addition, we plan to work with key stakeholders to enhance the promotion of the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme and review the scope of the Scheme. At the regional level, the HKMA will continue to collaborate with the International Finance Corporation through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks to roll out dedicated programmes in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing distinctive market insights, delivering targeted skills enhancement and training support, fostering community connections, facilitating potential green investment opportunities, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps for making green finance a core business. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has committed the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” to achieving net zero emissions by 2050 or earlier in support of the economy-wide transition. Through a pragmatic and rigorous responsible investment approach, we will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments, focusing primarily on the long-term resilience of its asset portfolio while exploring investment opportunities that can contribute to positive climate outcomes. The HKMA is committed to leading by example in corporate sustainability. In line with the accelerated timeline for meeting its net zero commitment announced in the “Action Agenda”, the HKMA will continue to advance corporate sustainability by progressively incorporating environmental and social factors into its strategies, risk assessments and reporting at a pragmatic pace. Specifically, in 2025 we will conduct a double materiality assessment to deepen our understanding of the potential financial and non-financial impacts of climate change and other sustainability issues, ensuring that we focus on material issues. In addition, we will conduct an energy audit and use technology solutions to assess the material impact of climate risk on our offices and operations, thereby enhancing our climate resilience and risk preparedness. We support the Government’s publication of the Roadmap on Sustainability Disclosure in Hong Kong and are actively preparing to make disclosures in accordance with the ISSB Standards. In 2025, the HKMA will remain committed to following the principles of energy efficiency and conservation in selecting data centres for planned upgrade projects. We will also expand digital initiatives to promote sustainability and enhance efficiency, including developing digital tools and platforms to support paperless processes and waste reduction, and improving the overall digital experience of our staff, banks and the public.

Climate change affects every aspect of human life, and everyone can contribute to mitigating its impact. Through its multiple roles as a central banking institution, banking regulator, market facilitator, responsible investor and sustainable organisation, the HKMA contributes to promoting and accelerating the transition to net zero in Hong Kong and across Asia. The HKMA has established a robust sustainability governance framework to guide the formulation of its relevant strategies and policies, oversee the implementation of related initiatives, and ensure that sustainability considerations are integrated into its own operations and practices. In pursuit of good corporate governance, the HKMA has established a robust sustainability governance framework for its sustainability-related work, with clear accountability arrangements and a high degree of transparency. The governance framework ensures that sustainability considerations are effectively incorporated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, with effective mechanisms in place to monitor and evaluate the progress and effectiveness of its sustainability work. The HKMA’s sustainability governance framework comprises: - the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant sub-committees, which monitor and advise on the HKMA’s work, including its sustainability work; - the Green and Sustainability Committee (GSC), chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, which steers the HKMA’s overall environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategies and policies at the management level; - for responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, which co-ordinates and oversees ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office; and - for other functional areas, relevant committees and working groups, which plan and implement sustainability initiatives relating to banking and market development as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (CASG), co-initiated by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), co-ordinates the efforts of financial regulators, government bureaux and departments, industry stakeholders and other stakeholders to accelerate the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. In view of the significant expansion in the scope of the HKMA’s sustainability work over the years, we established the GSC in October 2023 as a central platform to steer and more effectively co-ordinate all sustainability work across the HKMA’s different functional areas. - Provide guidance on the formulation of ESG-related strategies, policies and plans across four functional areas: banking, development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem, Exchange Fund investment and internal operations; - oversee the implementation of ESG-related plans by the HKMA’s functional departments; - assess the HKMA’s performance and effectiveness in achieving its ESG objectives; and - oversee external communication strategies. The GSC is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with the three Deputy Chief Executives serving as standing members. Executive Directors responsible for key functions relevant to green and sustainability matters are also invited to attend GSC meetings to report on major achievements and future plans relating to their work. The GSC meets regularly and is supported by relevant working groups under the HKMA’s banking departments, Corporate Development and Services Division, External Department and Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition to formulating and implementing its own sustainability initiatives, the HKMA and the SFC jointly initiated the CASG in May 2020. As a cross-agency platform, the CASG provides strategic direction and co-ordinates cross-sectoral efforts by the financial sector to address climate and environmental risks, with a view to reinforcing Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance centre in Asia and globally. For details of the CASG’s work, see the chapter “Enhancing the Green and Sustainable Finance Ecosystem”.

Climate change can pose risks to the financial system. The HKMA has been working to strengthen the resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system to climate risk, while contributing to Hong Kong’s climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to the impacts of various sustainability- and climate-related matters in their day-to-day operations and must therefore proactively manage climate risk. At the same time, banks play an important role in the financial system by directing capital towards green and sustainable projects. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has placed particular emphasis on building banks’ capacity to respond to and manage climate risk, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. In October, the HKMA published the “Sustainable Finance Action Agenda” (“Action Agenda”), setting out the HKMA’s vision to further consolidate Hong Kong’s position as the region’s sustainable finance hub and support sustainable development in Asia and globally. The “Action Agenda” sets out eight goals under four areas. To help the industry achieve the goals relating to banking policies, we have been undertaking the following initiatives. All banks strive to achieve net zero in their own operations by 2030 and in their financed emissions by 2050. All banks enhance transparency on climate-related risks and opportunities. In December, the HKMA shared good practices in transition planning with the industry and launched an industry consultation on the draft Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-2 “Transition Planning”. The new module aims to provide guidance on enhancing banks’ capabilities to address the net-zero transition and manage the associated risks. In addition, we are reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to incorporating into the assessment the relevant factors set out by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee) for the effective management of climate-related financial risks, and encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks, including transition planning, to address climate risk. The HKMA has been working to align local sustainability disclosure requirements with international standards, including the IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards (ISSB Standards) and the Basel Committee’s Pillar 3 disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks. Specifically, the HKMA is analysing the latest developments in sustainability disclosures and supporting the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants in conducting a technical feasibility study on adopting the ISSB Standards. Promoting green and transition finance is key to implementing the “Action Agenda”. In May, the HKMA published the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Taxonomy) to address industry concerns about greenwashing and help direct capital flows towards green and sustainable activities. The Taxonomy covers 12 economic activities under four sectors and is designed to align with the Common Ground Taxonomy and the taxonomies of Mainland China and the European Union, while incorporating elements relevant to local circumstances. We have commenced the second phase of work to expand the coverage of the Taxonomy and are consulting a broad range of stakeholders to further facilitate green and sustainable financing. During the year, the HKMA further strengthened its supervision of banks’ climate risk management and worked to support banks in building their capacity to manage climate-related risks and opportunities and address climate change. The HKMA also completed all initiatives under the two-year plan formulated in 2022 to incorporate climate risk into its banking supervisory processes. To help banks strengthen their climate risk management capabilities, the HKMA shared with the banking industry good practices observed in thematic examinations and consultation sessions, mainly including: - establishing robust governance frameworks that clearly define the responsibilities of boards of directors and senior management - ensuring effective oversight of key areas relating to climate-related risk matters: (1) facilitating and overseeing the effective formulation and implementation of climate strategies; (2) exercising appropriate oversight of climate-related risk management; and (3) fostering a sound climate risk culture within institutions. In August, the HKMA hosted a Balanced Supervision Roundtable with climate risk management as its theme. At the roundtable, bank representatives and HKMA participants exchanged views on various climate risk-related topics, including the challenges banks face in climate risk management, climate risk stress tests, transition planning and finance. The roundtable provided an interactive platform for information sharing and supported the HKMA’s work on climate risk supervision and other related areas. The HKMA launched a round of thematic examinations of banks’ climate risk management frameworks and practices, assessing their robustness and adequacy against the supervisory expectations set out in Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management”. The thematic examinations covered the entire risk management process, including risk identification, measurement, monitoring, reporting, control and mitigation, as well as climate risk scenario analysis and stress tests. The HKMA conducted a second series of consultation sessions to assess a new cohort of banks’ progress in implementing Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” and understand the challenges they faced. The consultation sessions also covered the latest regulatory and market developments in climate-related areas, including transition planning, disclosure frameworks and standards, and greenwashing issues. We provided feedback and guidance tailored to individual banks’ circumstances to support their climate risk management efforts. In 2024, the HKMA completed the second round of the banking sector Climate Risk Stress Test (CRST), with the participation of 21 retail banks and the Hong Kong branches of 25 international banking groups. The results showed that, under various scenarios, including one assuming the simultaneous occurrence of climate risk and a macroeconomic downturn, Hong Kong’s banking sector continued to demonstrate strong resilience to severe climate-related shocks. Compared with the CRST pilot exercise, participating banks significantly enhanced their capabilities in measuring and assessing climate risk. A report setting out the CRST results and good practices observed by the HKMA during the exercise was published in February 2025. The HKMA recognises the numerous data and methodological challenges banks face in managing climate risk, and has therefore been pursuing various initiatives to promote the use of technology to address these challenges. To address the lack of physical risk-related data and analytical tools for climate risk assessments, the HKMA launched the Physical Risk Assessment Platform in May, enabling banks to assess the potential impact of physical risk on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios. Looking ahead, the HKMA will enhance the platform in light of user feedback and by incorporating more local data. In addition, the HKMA collaborated with relevant stakeholders to promote the adoption of green fintech solutions by banks and the broader financial services industry. During the year, we published an adoption practice guide and two “Regtech Adoption Practice Guides” (English versions), illustrating technology solutions for environmental, social and governance (ESG) and sustainability assessments, as well as greenwashing risk management. We also hosted the third “FiNETech”, bringing together more than 150 financial institutions and technology companies to explore green fintech collaboration. Recognising that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its analysis and research on financial vulnerabilities to strengthen its ongoing surveillance. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analyses of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helped further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and supervisors to understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In November, the NGFS published the fifth vintage of its long-term climate macro-financial scenarios, providing a reference for forward-looking climate risk assessments. As a member of the Financial Stability Board’s Transition Plans Working Group, the HKMA participated in analysing the interactions between the transition plans of financial and non-financial companies and financial stability, enabling policymakers to examine climate-related financial risks from a forward-looking and dynamic perspective. The HKMA published the “Guide on the Use of Green Technologies in Banking” (English version), providing financial institutions with best practices in leveraging green technologies to facilitate their net-zero transition. On the research front, the HKMA conducted various applied research projects examining the impact of climate change on the financial sector and the broader economy. Research topics included the cross-border transmission of climate transition risk, the role of firms’ environmental performance in cushioning monetary policy shocks, the impact of climate-related factors on foreign direct investment flows, and the role of the financial sector in the transition towards a low-carbon economy. The findings not only deepened our understanding of how climate change affects financial stability, but also provided valuable insights into the green and sustainable finance ecosystem that support related policymaking. Locally, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate change on financial stability. The findings were also shared with a broad range of stakeholders through international forums and various channels, including HKMA Research Memorandums. The Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR), the research arm of the Hong Kong Academy of Finance, published a research paper on the impact of carbon pricing on corporate performance. The study provided evidence that low-emission firms can benefit significantly from carbon pricing, and highlighted its role in enhancing efficiency by reallocating resources from high-emission to low-emission firms. The study was featured in the HKIMR’s “Insights from Monetary Research” and shared with local and international academics and policy researchers. The HKMA’s “Liquidity Facilities Framework” is a collateralised standby facility that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA has incorporated sustainability considerations into the assessment of eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, we help facilitate international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, and draw insights from it to strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA is committed to raising market awareness and participation, providing the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and supporting relevant international initiatives to align with global standards. As set out in the HKMA’s “Sustainable Finance Action Agenda” (“Action Agenda”), the HKMA is committed to enhancing the green and sustainable finance ecosystem by mobilising capital for net zero and promoting more inclusive sustainability. Specifically, we are committed to establishing Hong Kong as the preferred sustainable financing platform for borrowers in the region and globally, supporting technological innovation in the green finance market, enhancing sustainability disclosures across the industry, expanding the local green talent pool, and addressing knowledge gaps in sustainable finance in Hong Kong and the region. Establish Hong Kong as the preferred sustainable financing platform in the region and globally Catalyse innovation in sustainable finance Support high-quality and comprehensive sustainability disclosures Address talent and knowledge gaps in sustainable finance in the region To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance and developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018. To date, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds totalling approximately US$28 billion equivalent to institutional and retail investors. The proceeds have been allocated to more than 110 government green projects, such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. We have capitalised on each issuance opportunity to continuously innovate and expand the features of green bonds, including their currencies, tenors and distribution channels, laying the groundwork for other public- and private-sector green bond issuers in the region. In 2024, to enhance the impact of the programme and further consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a green and sustainable finance hub, its scope was expanded to cover sustainable projects and it was renamed the “Government Sustainable Bond Programme” (Sustainable Bond Programme). To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Sustainable Bond Programme, the Government publishes a Green Bond Report annually, setting out in detail the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits. In July, the HKMA assisted the Government in issuing approximately US$3 billion equivalent of institutional green bonds under the Sustainable Bond Programme. The triple-currency offering comprised renminbi, US dollar and euro bonds of various tenors. The bonds attracted strong participation from a diverse range of investors, recording subscriptions of over US$15 billion equivalent. Among them, the 20- and 30-year renminbi green bonds were issued by the Government for the first time and were the Government’s longest-tenor renminbi bonds to date, providing new market benchmarks and further demonstrating the role of the Sustainable Bond Programme. These bonds also further broadened the range of offshore renminbi (CNH) investment products available in Hong Kong. Moreover, the strong response from global investors to the Government’s green bonds reflected their recognition of Hong Kong’s commitment to promoting green and sustainable development. To encourage more borrowers in the region to use Hong Kong’s financing platform to raise funds for sustainable development, the HKMA continued to implement the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme launched in May 2021, providing grants for eligible green and sustainable debt instruments issued in Hong Kong. The scheme has been well received by the industry. By the end of 2024, it had approved grants for approximately 500 green and sustainable debt instruments issued in Hong Kong with an aggregate value exceeding US$140 billion. In May 2024, the scheme was extended by three years to 2027, with its scope expanded to cover transition bonds and loans. The extension and expansion aim to encourage borrowers in relevant industries in the region to use Hong Kong’s transition finance platform to progressively decarbonise. - Grants approved for approximately 500 green and sustainable debt instruments issued in Hong Kong with an aggregate value exceeding US$140 billion (as at the end of 2024) - Extended by three years to 2027, with the scope expanded to cover transition finance instruments Meanwhile, the HKMA actively promoted Hong Kong’s sustainable financing platform, with encouraging results. In August, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong for the fourth time, totalling RMB7 billion, including RMB2.7 billion of green bonds, RMB1 billion of sustainability bonds and RMB900 million of social responsibility bonds. In September, the People’s Government of Guangdong Province issued offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, totalling RMB5 billion, including RMB1.5 billion of green bonds. In October, the Hainan Provincial People’s Government also issued offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the third time, totalling RMB3 billion, including RMB1 billion of blue bonds and RMB1 billion of sustainability bonds. These bond issuances once again highlighted Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable capital flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world. With these measures, Hong Kong consolidated its position as Asia’s preferred sustainable financing platform. According to statistics published by the International Capital Market Association, Hong Kong remained the largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances in Asia in 2024, with relevant bonds arranged in Hong Kong totalling US$43.1 billion, accounting for 45% of the regional total. To catalyse innovation in sustainable finance, the HKMA assisted the Government in issuing two landmark tokenised green bonds in 2023 and 2024, namely the world’s first tokenised government green bond and the world’s first multi-currency digital bond. These issuances demonstrated the Government’s support for regional market participants in applying asset digitalisation and innovative technologies in green and sustainable finance. In November, the HKMA also launched the Digital Bond Grant Scheme to promote digital bond issuances in Hong Kong, including digital green bonds, thereby encouraging and supporting innovation in Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance market. The working group on sustainability disclosures under the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) has been working towards adopting the International Financial Reporting Sustainability Disclosure Standards (ISSB Standards) in Hong Kong. In December 2024, the Government published the Roadmap on Sustainability Disclosure in Hong Kong, providing a clear pathway for large publicly accountable entities to fully adopt the ISSB Standards no later than 2028. The HKMA has been working closely with local and international partners to support entities at different stages of readiness in achieving high-quality sustainability disclosures, making such disclosures more accessible and inclusive. Notably, we continued to encourage the use of the Climate and Environmental Risk Questionnaire for Non-listed Companies (Questionnaire), launched by the Steering Group in collaboration with CDP in 2022. The Questionnaire provides an easy-to-use disclosure template to facilitate sustainability disclosures by businesses, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). An electronic version of the Questionnaire was launched in February 2024 to facilitate online completion by businesses (see the QR code below). The HKMA is refining the Questionnaire based on industry feedback and the latest international developments to make it more user-friendly, including by identifying core questions and providing common use cases. We are also seeking to improve the Questionnaire’s compatibility with other supporting tools on the Steering Group’s website. For more information about the Questionnaire, please visit the relevant webpage The HKMA leads by example by making high-quality sustainability disclosures in its Sustainability Report in accordance with the latest global standards, demonstrating its commitment. The report contains extensive information on the HKMA’s climate-related operational risks, its plans for achieving climate targets and implementation progress. For details of sustainability disclosures relating to our own operations, please refer to the chapter “A Sustainable HKMA”. Given the rapidly evolving sustainable finance market, the HKMA is strengthening skills training for the banking sector and facilitating knowledge sharing with other regulators and international stakeholders to address knowledge and talent gaps. To enhance the sustainable finance knowledge and skills of local banking practitioners, the HKMA and the Hong Kong Institute of Bankers (HKIB) launched the Foundation Level of the Green and Sustainable Finance module under the Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners in July 2023. The module aims to help banking professionals acquire knowledge and develop relevant professional competencies in green and sustainable finance more effectively, and covers four key work areas: (1) green and sustainable finance products and services; (2) sustainability/climate risk management; (3) sustainability disclosure and reporting; and (4) sustainability strategy, compliance and governance. In addition, the Professional Level of the Green and Sustainable Finance module, aimed at middle- to senior-level banking practitioners responsible for relevant work, was launched in November. To provide banking practitioners with the necessary training, the HKIB, as the administrator of the Green and Sustainable Finance module, launched the Foundation Level training programme in May. Following the launch of the Professional Level in November, the HKMA will work with the banking industry in 2025 to develop its training programme. To understand the banking industry’s further skills and training needs, the HKMA is currently working with the industry on the “Capacity Building for Future Banking 2026–2030” study, with a view to publishing the findings in 2025. This joint study follows up on the “Capacity Building for Future Banking 2021–2025” document published in June 2020. The findings of the follow-up study will provide an important reference for the industry in formulating and adjusting talent training strategies and initiatives to support the sustainable development of the banking sector. Through collaboration with the Steering Group, the HKMA also continued to support the implementation of the Government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme, which subsidises practitioners, graduates and students undertaking sustainable finance-related training. As of December 2024, 85 international and local programmes had been registered as eligible training programmes under the scheme, and more than 5,700 reimbursement applications had been approved. The Government announced in the 2025–26 Budget that the scheme would be extended to 2028. The HKMA is committed to leveraging its experience to promote skills training and knowledge sharing through regional and international collaboration. As a founding member of the Capacity-building Alliance of Sustainable Investment (CASI), the HKMA Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office co-organised a two-day training workshop with CASI in Hong Kong in June, with discussions focusing on global sustainable finance markets, policy frameworks and innovative instruments. In addition, the HKMA supported the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ) in establishing a chapter in Hong Kong in October, and will leverage GFANZ’s network and expertise to strengthen skills training in transition planning and transition finance.

As an important global asset owner and manager, the HKMA actively leads the development of green and sustainable finance. Drawing on its experience in demonstrating that financial performance and positive impact can reinforce each other, the HKMA adheres to responsible investment principles in managing the Exchange Fund, prioritises sustainable assets, and requires its external investment managers to exercise active ownership. Investing prudently in accordance with the principle of “capital preservation first, long-term value creation”, the HKMA believes that giving due consideration to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors helps mitigate relevant investment risks while unlocking the long-term sustainable value of investments. As a committed signatory to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA is dedicated to advancing its responsible investment efforts. We place particular emphasis on sustainability, especially the pressing issue of climate change, with the aim of enhancing the resilience of the Exchange Fund and achieving better risk-adjusted long-term returns. We integrate ESG factors in a pragmatic and orderly manner and continue to explore a range of investment instruments to channel capital towards sustainable investments across different asset classes (Figure 1). Leveraging its role as a major investor, the HKMA contributes to advancing the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. In September, the HKMA published the “HKMA ESG Expectations” and made the document available to investment partners through its annual ESG workshop and the HKMA website. We collaborate with like-minded investors, regulators and international organisations to develop industry standards and promote the adoption of responsible investment across the financial sector and central banking community. Through these collaborative efforts, we strive to foster a future in which finance and sustainable development progress in tandem. In October, the HKMA announced the “Sustainable Finance Action Agenda” (“Action Agenda”), articulating its commitment to further investing in a sustainable future by achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” by 2050 or earlier and mobilising partners to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The overarching guiding principle sets the tone for the HKMA to pursue responsible investment while taking into account the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing the ESG and climate-related risks associated with Exchange Fund investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors their implementation through regular meeting reports from the Sustainable Investment Team of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 2, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Strategy Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing the Exchange Fund Investment Office’s various ESG initiatives. Proposals and work progress discussed at the ESG Committee’s quarterly meetings are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. In addition, the Green and Sustainability Steering Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and attended by the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, meets regularly to provide guidance on ESG policies and measures across the HKMA’s different functions, including the Exchange Fund Investment Office, in pursuit of the HKMA’s overall ESG objectives. The Sustainable Investment Team works closely with different teams in the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG, particularly climate-related, risks and opportunities across various investments: - Public market investments – The Credit, Regulatory and Monitoring Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, reviews the integration of ESG factors into credit risk models with input from the Sustainable Investment Team, and monitors the ESG profile of fixed-income portfolios through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Department. The Sustainable Investment Team also participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring of external investment managers for equity portfolios (see “Promoting active ownership” under the “Risk management” section on page 39 for details). - Private market investments – The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments of each investment proposal made by the private market investment and risk management teams. The HKMA recognises that the physical and transition risks arising from climate change, as well as the associated opportunities, will affect the long-term financial performance of Exchange Fund investments. The Emissions Gap Report 2024 published by the United Nations Environment Programme projects that the global average temperature will rise by 2.6 to 3.1 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels unless there is rapid and large-scale global mobilisation to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Uncertainty over policy changes, technological developments and behavioural shifts in response to rising temperatures may intensify transition risks, resulting in greater market volatility and affecting asset valuations. At the same time, the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events also pose additional risks of physical damage and financial loss to investments. Amid these challenges, the shift by governments and industries towards sustainable solutions also creates investment opportunities with potentially attractive long-term prospects in low-carbon solutions, emerging technologies and sustainable infrastructure. The HKMA believes that investing in a sustainable future is consistent with the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund and therefore places particular emphasis on climate-related considerations in its ESG integration. The HKMA has set a target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” by 2050 or earlier and continues to advance its efforts through an orderly three-pronged approach to achieve this target (see Figure 3). In 2024, the HKMA announced the “Action Agenda”, which reinforced the Exchange Fund’s climate transition-related commitments and efforts (see Figure 4). To support the transition to a low-carbon economy, the HKMA favours active engagement over exclusion or divestment from the investable universe. Investing in a sustainable future Achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio” by 2050 or earlier - Actively expand the scope and range of sustainable investments, particularly climate transition-themed investments in public and private markets - Integrate ESG factors into every investment decision, with particular attention to climate change and transition outlook considerations - Establish clear ESG expectations aligned with international standards and best practices, and require all external investment managers, investee companies and counterparties to follow them - Strive to reduce the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio by 67% from the 2017 level by 2030 or earlier Supporting the region’s transition through investment - Continue engaging with external investment managers to optimise transition-enabling investment opportunities - Continue identifying and prioritising quality investment opportunities that can facilitate Asia’s transition and deliver positive global impact First, maintaining a diversified and robust asset portfolio is critical to achieving the Exchange Fund’s primary investment objectives. Directly excluding certain sectors or industries would narrow the investable universe, with potential implications for investment returns and risks. Through an inclusive approach, the HKMA can capture opportunities to invest in companies that are undergoing transition and possess superior technologies and sound corporate governance to respond to evolving global climate trends, including companies in high-emitting industries. Second, tackling climate change requires the transition of core “brown” industries. Merely excluding or divesting from relevant investments does not help solve the problem of carbon emissions. Instead, the HKMA supports these industries through strategic capital deployment and active ownership, encouraging them to transition towards sustainable and low-carbon practices and thereby bringing about positive change for themselves and the world. Net-zero investment approaches have evolved from favouring green or low-carbon assets to encompassing assets with credible transition prospects, thereby driving comprehensive decarbonisation across the entire economy. As a global asset owner, the HKMA recognises that the long-term resilience of an asset portfolio depends not only on adjustments within the portfolio itself, but also on a broad-based economic transition. While there is no single perfect solution, the HKMA enhanced its responsible investment strategy in 2024 by adopting a comprehensive and diversified approach to driving the transition while supporting the Exchange Fund’s and global net-zero goals. The strategy combines top-down and bottom-up tools, including ESG integration and stewardship in fundamental analysis, portfolio decarbonisation tilts, and thematic investments targeting a range of assets aligned with pathways towards net-zero emissions. In public markets, this may involve tilting portfolios towards ESG leaders or companies providing climate solutions, complemented by stewardship to facilitate corporate transition. In private markets, greater emphasis may be placed on transition-enabling investments. By integrating ESG factors into investment decisions, the HKMA continues to identify investment opportunities that can facilitate the climate transition while enhancing the long-term resilience of the Exchange Fund’s asset portfolios. Sustainable investments across different asset classes account for more than 10% of the Exchange Fund’s “Investment Portfolio”, with financial performance comparable to the relevant portfolio benchmarks (Figure 5). - Public market investments – The HKMA launched an actively managed global equity portfolio focused on sustainability and climate transition, and extended the use of a customised low-carbon equity index to two additional portfolios managed by external investment managers. The HKMA also continues to seek green, social and sustainability (GSS) bonds that provide competitive returns while financing sustainable projects (see the “Enhancing sustainability through GSS bonds” section for related case studies). - Private market investments – The HKMA is committed to building a resilient long-term growth portfolio and capturing investment opportunities aligned with climate and energy transition themes. Leveraging its extensive network and expertise, the HKMA also actively identifies and assesses investment opportunities that can accelerate the energy transition, including through strategic partnerships with multinational organisations (see the “Joining forces to tackle climate challenges in Asia and globally” section for examples). - Passive portfolios benchmarked against ESG indices - Customised decarbonisation strategies for passive and actively managed quantitative portfolios whose benchmarks are not ESG indices - Governance-themed actively managed portfolios - Sustainability- and climate transition-themed actively managed ESG portfolios - Projects with sustainable characteristics, such as renewable energy infrastructure and green-certified buildings and warehouses - Funds focused on energy transition and decarbonisation globally, in Asia and in the Global South - Green, social and sustainability bonds - A green bond fund managed by an international organisation - The Managed Co-Lending Portfolio Program (MCPP), managed by the International Finance Corporation and focused on sustainable projects in emerging markets - The “MCPP One Planet” programme, providing Paris Agreement-aligned climate-related investments in emerging markets The HKMA invested in green bonds issued by a quasi-governmental institution. The proceeds from the green bonds were allocated to several projects, including the upgrading of ageing equipment at several wastewater treatment facilities. These upgrades included enhancing monitoring and control systems and pump performance to generate positive environmental benefits from wastewater management, waste reduction and recycling processes. In addition to the continued treatment of wastewater and sludge, these facilities compost or repurpose dewatered sludge to produce fertiliser, charcoal, cement and other construction materials, achieving a sludge recycling rate of up to 100%. The facilities also use gas generated during sludge treatment to fuel boilers and generate electricity. The HKMA invested in green bonds issued by a multilateral development bank. The bonds financed several projects, including the rehabilitation of a country’s canal system. As one of the country’s largest irrigation systems, the canal is designed to divert excess river flows to arid areas. The project’s main objective is to rehabilitate the deteriorating canal lining to prevent seepage, conserve water, improve water-use efficiency and reclaim waterlogged areas. In addition, the project provides skills training to local stakeholders to promote the adoption and effective use of modern irrigation technologies, such as micro-irrigation, and sustainable farming practices.

The HKMA is committed to being a responsible and sustainable organisation. One of the HKMA’s key priorities in 2024 in delivering on this commitment was its plan to bring forward the target date for achieving net-zero emissions in its corporate operations to 2030, 20 years earlier than originally targeted and in line with the Sustainable Finance Action Agenda. In addition to promoting environmental sustainability, the HKMA is committed to fostering staff development and well-being, and strives to promote financial inclusion and enhance public financial literacy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Green and Sustainability Steering Committee (Steering Committee) is the principal decision-making body for corporate sustainability initiatives. To demonstrate the HKMA’s commitment to climate change, the Steering Committee endorsed in October 2024 a new target for the HKMA to achieve net-zero emissions in its corporate operations by 2030 as part of the Sustainable Finance Action Agenda (Action Agenda). At the departmental level, the Executive Director (Corporate Services) provides guidance on implementing sustainability initiatives relating to corporate operations, staff well-being and social engagement, and reports regularly to the Steering Committee. The Administration Division serves as the coordinator and central hub for implementing, communicating and reporting corporate sustainability initiatives. An additional layer of support is provided by the Green Office Box Group and Volunteer Services Group, comprising staff from different operational departments; the former serves as a platform for brainstorming and proposing ideas on creating a green workplace, while the latter aims to foster a culture of staff participation in volunteer activities. In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, its staff and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the “15 Years Plus Caring Organisation” logo for 18 consecutive years from 2006 to 2024. The HKMA’s sustainability strategy continues to be structured around the three pillars of environmental, people and social responsibility. - Focus on decarbonising and digitalising the HKMA’s daily operations, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030 - Adopt green procurement requirements in accordance with Government guidelines - Promote greener operating practices across the financial industry and wider society - Build an engaged workforce and talent pool to achieve the HKMA’s strategic objectives - Foster a collaborative, caring and inclusive work environment that values diversity and strengthens staff’s sense of belonging - Provide a quality work environment that promotes a healthy lifestyle - Foster a caring culture - Incorporate social considerations into procurement processes and supply chain management - Promote financial inclusion and enhance public financial literacy through consumer education initiatives The HKMA cares about climate change and leads by example. In October 2024, the HKMA announced its plan to bring forward the target date for achieving net-zero emissions in its corporate operations to 2030, 20 years earlier than its original commitment, as part of the Action Agenda. The HKMA has revised its roadmap for the net-zero transition, focusing on responsibly managing the environmental impact of its daily operations through reducing carbon emissions, saving energy and paper, and recycling waste, while taking full advantage of improvements in the fuel mix for electricity generation by local power companies. The HKMA has also created a digital workplace to enhance efficiency while reducing its carbon footprint. Moreover, recognising the importance of fostering a sustainability culture, the HKMA encourages staff to actively adopt sustainability-friendly practices through ongoing promotional programmes and activities. Under its overarching 2030 net-zero target, the HKMA has been exploring the use of carbon insetting tools within its own value chain to reduce emissions and procuring low-carbon products and services wherever possible. In this regard, since 2023 the HKMA has fully offset the carbon emissions from air travel by purchasing sustainable aviation fuel and participating in carbon offsetting programmes. The HKMA will expand its carbon insetting and offsetting programmes to cover all other major carbon emissions. In addition to the above environmental commitments relating to its physical operations, the HKMA continues to promote the market’s low-carbon transition through initiatives ranging from introducing electronic document submission and processing procedures to facilitating electronic payments and collecting coins for recirculation. The remainder of this chapter details the HKMA’s strategies for environmental leadership, promoting staff well-being and caring for society. Under the HKMA’s overall enterprise risk management framework, the Risk Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for monitoring and reviewing the potential risks and threats that the HKMA faces in its daily operations, including those arising from climate change. To assess more effectively the potential operational impacts of climate change, the HKMA has identified various climate-related risks and reviewed their actual and potential impacts. To address climate-related risks while ensuring operational continuity, the HKMA’s offices incorporate various measures into their design to mitigate potential physical hazards, fires and other emergencies. The HKMA also regularly updates its contingency plans to incorporate comprehensive measures covering not only its offices but also communications and computer facilities. Evacuation and backup facility activation drills are conducted regularly to ensure staff are always prepared to implement contingency measures.
